# 4. The data you store

Everything lives in one Postgres database (S4). The record tables are the portal's own, extended with sync
metadata. Everything that exists only for the sync lives in a separate `sync` schema owned by the sync code.
Labels like `D15` and `T1` point to [decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md).

## 4.1 Overview

| Table | What it holds | Written by | Rows | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `customers`, `contacts` | Current values, plus per-field metadata in `field_meta` | portal backend, receiver, worker | 5M together | about 5 GB, plus about 1 GB of indexes |
| `history` | One row per field change, append-only, partitioned by month | all three | about 60 GB/year at a realistic 10 edits/s | 13 months kept, then archived (D15) |
| `sync.inbox` | Webhooks received in the last 7 days, partitioned by day | receiver | about 18M at peak | about 2.7 GB (T4) |
| `sync.outbox` | Portal changes waiting for, or recently sent to, Salesforce | portal backend, worker | one pending row per record, plus 7 days of sent rows | about 216 MB pending after a 6-hour outage (D21) |
| `sync.jobs` | Salesforce calls the receiver needs but may not make | receiver, worker | hundreds | tiny |
| `sync.heartbeat` | Last time each receiver could write | receiver | one per receiver | tiny |
| `sync.watermarks` | The reconciliation sweep's "modified since" point | worker | a few | tiny |

## 4.2 Records: `customers` and `contacts` (T1, T2)

```
customers
  id               uuid  PK            -- portal's own ID; also sent as Portal_Id__c (D8)
  sf_id            char(18) NULL       -- Salesforce Account ID once known (D9); unique when set
  name             text
  status           text                -- Account.Status__c
  owner_sf_id      char(18)            -- Account.OwnerId, a Salesforce user ID (D10)
  field_meta       jsonb               -- per-field metadata, below
  sf_version       bigint NULL         -- newest record-level sequence we have seen (G1 precondition)
  sf_last_modified timestamptz NULL    -- Salesforce LastModifiedDate (fallback version, G3)
  created_at, updated_at timestamptz

contacts
  id, sf_id, field_meta, sf_version, sf_last_modified, created_at, updated_at   -- as above
  first_name       text                -- Contact.FirstName  (brief's "full name" is two fields, S1)
  last_name        text                -- Contact.LastName
  phone            text                -- Contact.Phone
  email            text                -- Contact.Email
  city             text                -- Contact.MailingCity
  owner_sf_id      char(18)            -- Contact.OwnerId
  customer_id      uuid NULL FK -> customers.id   -- NULL while the customer is pending (D14)
  customer_sf_id   char(18) NULL       -- Contact.AccountId, always as Salesforce sent it
```

**`field_meta`**: one entry for each synced field, holding what the apply rule needs:

```json
{
  "city":  { "updatedAt": "2026-11-22T10:00:00.120Z", "source": "portal",
             "actor": "portal:u_17", "sfSeq": 40, "sfValue": "Mumbai" },
  "phone": { "updatedAt": "2026-11-22T10:00:05.000Z", "source": "salesforce",
             "actor": "sf:005XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX", "sfSeq": 42, "sfValue": "+91 98100 00000" }
}
```

| Key | Meaning | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `updatedAt` | The time used to decide conflicts: Salesforce `occurredAt`, or the portal's time inside the save transaction, taken after the record lock | D16 |
| `source` | `portal` or `salesforce` | D16 tie-break, badge |
| `actor` | Portal user ID or Salesforce user ID, prefixed with its side | history, badge |
| `sfSeq` | The Salesforce `sequence` that last set this field | D19 out-of-order rule |
| `sfValue` | The last value Salesforce is known to hold. Set when a webhook is applied and when a send is confirmed | D10 revert after a rejection |

**Indexes:**
- `customers(sf_id)` and `contacts(sf_id)`: unique where not NULL. Webhooks look records up by this.
- `contacts(customer_id)`.
- `contacts(customer_sf_id) WHERE customer_id IS NULL`: finds waiting contacts when their customer arrives.

**Why a JSONB column, not more columns or a separate table** (T1):
- The portal reads and filters plain typed columns.
- The metadata is one row, so one lock (G2) and one write, and it loads straight into the apply function.
- Postgres doesn't enforce the JSONB shape, so the apply function validates it.

## 4.3 `history` (D15, S3b)

Append-only. Rows are inserted and never updated.

```
history                                   -- PARTITION BY RANGE (recorded_at), one partition per month
  id            bigint identity
  record_type   text                      -- customer | contact
  record_id     uuid
  field         text
  old_value     jsonb
  new_value     jsonb
  actor         text                      -- portal:u_17 | sf:005...
  source        text                      -- portal | salesforce
  via           text                      -- portal_save | webhook | fetch | replay | reconcile (S3b)
  occurred_at   timestamptz               -- the time the conflict rule compared
  recorded_at   timestamptz               -- when we wrote the row
  event_id      text NULL                 -- webhook / replay event
  change_id     text NULL                 -- Portal_Change_Id__c of a portal save
  sf_seq        bigint NULL
  superseded    boolean                   -- this value lost at the moment it arrived (older sequence or earlier time)
  note          text NULL                 -- e.g. "rejected by Salesforce: <reason>", "normalised by Salesforce"
```

- **Index:** `(record_id, recorded_at)`. History is read one record at a time (D15).
- **`superseded` is decided when the row is inserted**, because the apply rule knows at that moment whether
  the value won. A value that was current and is later replaced is ordinary history, not superseded. That
  is what keeps the table append-only.
- **Retention:** 13 monthly partitions in Postgres. Older ones are detached and archived to object storage,
  never deleted. About 200 B per row, about 0.9 GB per day at peak, and about 65–80 GB in Postgres in total.
- **The UI badge** (D16, G1b) is a query on this table: the latest rows for a field, compared by
  `occurred_at`.

## 4.4 `sync.inbox` (D18, T4)

```
sync.inbox                               -- PARTITION BY RANGE (received_day), one partition per day
  event_id      text
  received_day  date
  record_id     char(18)
  sequence      bigint
  received_at   timestamptz
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, received_day)
  UNIQUE (record_id, sequence, received_day)
```

- The receiver does `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Zero rows inserted means a duplicate: reply `200`
  and stop.
- **Each night the oldest partition is dropped.** That is instant and leaves no dead space.
- A duplicate that arrives on a **later day** lands in a different partition, so it passes this check. The
  per-field `sequence` rule (D19) then rejects its fields. The worst case is an extra history row marked
  superseded, never a wrong value.
- We store only the keys, not the body, so a webhook for a record is never applied twice and the table
  stays small.

## 4.5 `sync.outbox` (D23, T3, G1, G2b)

```
sync.outbox
  id               bigint identity PK
  record_type      text
  record_id        uuid                 -- our record (Portal_Id__c)
  op               text                 -- upsert (create) | update
  fields           jsonb                -- merged pending values: {"city": "Noida", "phone": "..."}
  change_id        text NULL            -- Portal_Change_Id__c; fixed when claimed, reused on every retry
  base_version     bigint NULL          -- record version sent as the precondition (G1)
  status           text                 -- pending | sending | sent | rejected
  attempts         int
  consecutive_412  int                  -- back off after 5 (G1b)
  next_attempt_at  timestamptz
  created_at       timestamptz          -- picks the lane after an outage (D21)
  claimed_at       timestamptz NULL     -- rows 'sending' for > 60 s are resent (G2b)
  last_error       text NULL
```

- **One pending row per record:** `UNIQUE (record_id) WHERE status = 'pending'`. A save does
  `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (record_id) WHERE status = 'pending' DO UPDATE SET fields = outbox.fields || EXCLUDED.fields`.
  A `sending` row doesn't count, so an edit made during a send starts a new pending row.
- **Claiming:** index on `(next_attempt_at) WHERE status = 'pending'`.
- **Sent rows** are kept 7 days, for echo matching and support, then deleted in small batches every minute.
  That keeps the delete load steady. This table can't be partitioned the way the inbox is, because the
  one-pending-row index must cover the whole table.
- **Size:** about 500 B per row. After a 6-hour outage: 432,000 pending rows, about 216 MB, less with
  merging (D21). Seven days of sent rows at a sustained portal peak of 20/s would be about 12M rows, about
  6 GB. At realistic rates it's well under that.

## 4.6 `sync.jobs` (D14, S3, D19)

```
sync.jobs
  id           bigint identity PK
  type         text          -- fetch_customer | fetch_record | replay_record
  record_type  text
  sf_id        char(18)
  run_at       timestamptz   -- 5 s / 15 s / 25 s schedule for fetches; +10 s for a gap replay
  attempts     int
  status       text          -- pending | running | done | failed
  created_at   timestamptz
  UNIQUE (type, sf_id) WHERE status = 'pending'     -- one pending job of each kind per record
```

Finished jobs are deleted after 1 day. They use the 20 req/s headroom, never the 80 req/s outbox share.

## 4.7 `sync.heartbeat` and `sync.watermarks` (G3, G4)

```
sync.heartbeat    receiver_id text PK, beat_at timestamptz        -- updated every 5 s by each receiver
sync.watermarks   name text PK, value timestamptz                 -- 'sweep:customers', 'sweep:contacts'
```

- **After a database outage**, the worker replays the change log from `min(beat_at)` taken just before the
  outage, minus 10 minutes (G4).
- **The sweep** reads records modified since `value` minus an overlap, then advances `value` (G3).
- A heartbeat is a timer write, not a write per webhook, so 30 webhooks/s never queue up on one row.

## 4.8 Who may touch what (S4, G2b)

| Postgres role | Records | `history` | `inbox` | `outbox` | `jobs` | `heartbeat` / `watermarks` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `portal_app` | read / write through `saveEdit()` | insert, select | – | insert, merge pending | – | – |
| `receiver` | read / write | insert | insert | **none** (loop rule, D17) | insert | heartbeat: write |
| `worker` | read / write | insert | – | read / write | read / write | read / write |

Each role has `lock_timeout = 2s`, `statement_timeout = 5s` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 5s`
(G2b). Migrations run under their own role.

## 4.9 What is on disk after the 6-hour outage

The outage leaves about **432,000 pending outbox rows (about 216 MB)** in `sync.outbox`. They survive any
restart because they sit in Postgres and are written in the same transaction as the edit. Webhooks that
did arrive are already applied, and the rest come back through replay. The drain is covered in
section 10.

Append-only. Rows are inserted and never updated.

```
history                                   -- PARTITION BY RANGE (recorded_at), one partition per month
  id            bigint identity
  record_type   text                      -- customer | contact
  record_id     uuid
  field         text
  old_value     jsonb
  new_value     jsonb
  actor         text                      -- portal:u_17 | sf:005...
  source        text                      -- portal | salesforce
  via           text                      -- portal_save | webhook | fetch | replay | reconcile (S3b)
  occurred_at   timestamptz               -- the time the conflict rule compared
  recorded_at   timestamptz               -- when we wrote the row
  event_id      text NULL                 -- webhook / replay event
  change_id     text NULL                 -- Portal_Change_Id__c of a portal save
  sf_seq        bigint NULL
  superseded    boolean                   -- this value lost at the moment it arrived (older sequence or earlier time)
  note          text NULL                 -- e.g. "rejected by Salesforce: <reason>", "normalised by Salesforce"
```

- **Index:** `(record_id, recorded_at)`. History is read one record at a time (D15).
- **`superseded` is decided when the row is inserted**, because the apply rule knows at that moment whether
  the value won. A value that was current and is later replaced is ordinary history, not superseded. That
  is what keeps the table append-only.
- **Retention:** 13 monthly partitions in Postgres. Older ones are detached and archived to object storage,
  never deleted. About 200 B per row, about 0.9 GB per day at peak, and about 65–80 GB in Postgres in total.
- **The UI badge** (D16, G1b) is a query on this table: the latest rows for a field, compared by
  `occurred_at`.

## 4.4 `sync.inbox` (D18, T4)

```
sync.inbox                               -- PARTITION BY RANGE (received_day), one partition per day
  event_id      text
  received_day  date
  record_id     char(18)
  sequence      bigint
  received_at   timestamptz
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, received_day)
  UNIQUE (record_id, sequence, received_day)
```

- The receiver does `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Zero rows inserted means a duplicate: reply `200`
  and stop.
- **Each night the oldest partition is dropped.** That is instant and leaves no dead space.
- A duplicate that arrives on a **later day** lands in a different partition, so it passes this check. The
  per-field `sequence` rule (D19) then rejects its fields. The worst case is an extra history row marked
  superseded, never a wrong value.
- We store only the keys, not the body, so a webhook for a record is never applied twice and the table
  stays small.

## 4.5 `sync.outbox` (D23, T3, G1, G2b)

```
sync.outbox
  id               bigint identity PK
  record_type      text
  record_id        uuid                 -- our record (Portal_Id__c)
  op               text                 -- upsert (create) | update
  fields           jsonb                -- merged pending values: {"city": "Noida", "phone": "..."}
  change_id        text NULL            -- Portal_Change_Id__c; fixed when claimed, reused on every retry
  base_version     bigint NULL          -- record version sent as the precondition (G1)
  status           text                 -- pending | sending | sent | rejected
  attempts         int
  consecutive_412  int                  -- back off after 5 (G1b)
  next_attempt_at  timestamptz
  created_at       timestamptz          -- picks the lane after an outage (D21)
  claimed_at       timestamptz NULL     -- rows 'sending' for > 60 s are resent (G2b)
  last_error       text NULL
```

- **One pending row per record:** `UNIQUE (record_id) WHERE status = 'pending'`. A save does
  `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (record_id) WHERE status = 'pending' DO UPDATE SET fields = outbox.fields || EXCLUDED.fields`.
  A `sending` row doesn't count, so an edit made during a send starts a new pending row.
- **Claiming:** index on `(next_attempt_at) WHERE status = 'pending'`.
- **Sent rows** are kept 7 days, for echo matching and support, then deleted in small batches every minute.
  That keeps the delete load steady. This table can't be partitioned the way the inbox is, because the
  one-pending-row index must cover the whole table.
- **Size:** about 500 B per row. After a 6-hour outage: 432,000 pending rows, about 216 MB, less with
  merging (D21). Seven days of sent rows at a sustained portal peak of 20/s would be about 12M rows, about
  6 GB. At realistic rates it's well under that.

## 4.6 `sync.jobs` (D14, S3, D19)

```
sync.jobs
  id           bigint identity PK
  type         text          -- fetch_customer | fetch_record | replay_record
  record_type  text
  sf_id        char(18)
  run_at       timestamptz   -- 5 s / 15 s / 25 s schedule for fetches; +10 s for a gap replay
  attempts     int
  status       text          -- pending | running | done | failed
  created_at   timestamptz
  UNIQUE (type, sf_id) WHERE status = 'pending'     -- one pending job of each kind per record
```

Finished jobs are deleted after 1 day. They use the 20 req/s headroom, never the 80 req/s outbox share.

## 4.7 `sync.heartbeat` and `sync.watermarks` (G3, G4)

```
sync.heartbeat    receiver_id text PK, beat_at timestamptz        -- updated every 5 s by each receiver
sync.watermarks   name text PK, value timestamptz                 -- 'sweep:customers', 'sweep:contacts'
```

- **After a database outage**, the worker replays the change log from `min(beat_at)` taken just before the
  outage, minus 10 minutes (G4).
- **The sweep** reads records modified since `value` minus an overlap, then advances `value` (G3).
- A heartbeat is a timer write, not a write per webhook, so 30 webhooks/s never queue up on one row.

## 4.8 Who may touch what (S4, G2b)

| Postgres role | Records | `history` | `inbox` | `outbox` | `jobs` | `heartbeat` / `watermarks` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `portal_app` | read / write through `saveEdit()` | insert, select | – | insert, merge pending | – | – |
| `receiver` | read / write | insert | insert | **none** (loop rule, D17) | insert | heartbeat: write |
| `worker` | read / write | insert | – | read / write | read / write | read / write |

Each role has `lock_timeout = 2s`, `statement_timeout = 5s` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 5s`
(G2b). Migrations run under their own role.

## 4.9 What is on disk after the 6-hour outage

The outage leaves about **432,000 pending outbox rows (about 216 MB)** in `sync.outbox`. They survive any
restart because they sit in Postgres and are written in the same transaction as the edit. Webhooks that
did arrive are already applied, and the rest come back through replay. The drain is covered in
section 10.

# Tequity Round 1 - Salesforce <-> portal sync

Design docs live in `docs/`: decisions in `decisions.tmp.md`, assumptions in `assumptions.md`,
build order in `subproblems.md`. Decision labels (`Dn`, `Sn`) point into `decisions.tmp.md`.

## Shared database and `saveEdit()` module (decision S4) - keep these rules when changing code

The portal backend, the webhook receiver and the sync worker share one Postgres database. A portal
edit writes the record, its history and the outbox row in **one transaction** through a shared
`saveEdit()` module. That transaction is what stops a crash from losing an edit or sending an
unsaved one (D23). The costs we accepted, and the rules that contain them:

1. **Every portal write goes through `saveEdit()`.** A direct `UPDATE` on a records table skips the
   outbox, and that edit silently never reaches Salesforce. A test must fail if a record row changes
   without a matching outbox row. Never bypass it, even for scripts or admin fixes.
2. **The webhook path never writes to the outbox** (loop rule, D17). Do not add a database trigger
   that writes the outbox on every update: it would also fire on webhook writes.
3. **Sync tables live in their own `sync` schema** (`inbox`, `outbox`, `jobs`). The sync code owns
   their migrations; the portal only calls the module.
4. **Same language:** the module is TypeScript on Node (20+), the portal backend's language.
5. **Each service has its own capped connection pool** (e.g. receiver 10, worker 5), so a webhook
   burst or an outage drain cannot starve portal users.
6. **A failed outbox insert fails the user's save.** This is deliberate: a save that cannot be
   synced must not look saved.
7. **One Postgres role per service, least privilege.** For example, the receiver cannot touch
   `outbox`; the worker never receives HTTP; the receiver never calls Salesforce (D22).

## Locking and the Salesforce precondition (decisions G1, G2, G2b) - keep these rules

1. **Every write to per-field state goes through `withRecordLock(recordId, fn)`**: lock the record row
   (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), read, run the pure apply function, write, commit. No other way to open a
   transaction on records.
2. **Never call Salesforce inside a transaction.** The Salesforce client throws when called inside
   `withRecordLock`; keep that check and its test. The worker sends in three steps: claim (tx) -> HTTP
   call (no tx) -> store result (tx).
3. **Lock order:** customer before contact, then by ID. Deadlock victims retry.
4. **One record per transaction** for replay, drain and sweep. Bulk work (e.g. linking contacts to a
   newly arrived customer) runs in batches of 500, each its own transaction.
5. **Keep transactions to database writes only.** Emails, HTTP calls and other side effects happen
   after the commit.
6. **Postgres timeouts per role:** `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 5s`, `lock_timeout = 2s`,
   `statement_timeout = 5s`. Migrations use their own role with a `lock_timeout`.
7. **Every update to Salesforce is conditional** on the record version we last saw. On `412`: GET the
   record; if its `Portal_Change_Id__c` is ours, our write already landed; otherwise re-run the
   conflict rule per field and resend only the winners. Never retry a lost field automatically; the
   user overrides with "Use my value again".
8. **Replay restarts from a heartbeat minus an overlap**, never from "the last `eventId` we applied"
   (webhooks arrive out of order).

## Other fixed rules

- Only one sync worker is active at a time (Postgres advisory lock, standby takes over). The rate
  limiter is in memory; do not scale the worker horizontally without a shared limiter.
- Contact full name is stored as `first_name` / `last_name` (Salesforce `Contact.Name` is read-only).

T1–T4 are recorded in [decisions.tmp.md](docs/decisions.tmp.md:261), and outline item 4 is written as [docs/data.md](docs/data.md).

**What the section covers:**
- **4.1 Overview:** every table, who writes it, how many rows, and how big it gets. Records about 6 GB with indexes, history about 65–80 GB, inbox about 2.7 GB, and outbox about 216 MB after an outage.
- **4.2 Records:** the column lists for customers and contacts.
  - The ID is a UUID that doubles as `Portal_Id__c`. `sf_id` is unique when set.
  - Contacts carry `customer_id` and `customer_sf_id`, so "customer pending" is visible.
  - `sf_version` holds the record version used for the G1 precondition.
  - The `field_meta` JSON shape is shown with an example, plus what each key is used for.
- **4.3 History:** the columns, monthly partitions, the index, and retention.
- **4.4–4.7:** the inbox (daily partitions), outbox (the unique pending-row index and the merge SQL), jobs, heartbeat and watermarks.
- **4.8:** which Postgres role may touch which table. The receiver has no access to the outbox, which enforces the loop rule in the database.
- **4.9:** what's on disk after the outage, linking ahead to section 10.

**Two details I added while writing. Please check them:**
1. **`sfValue` in `field_meta`:** the last value Salesforce is known to hold for each field. D10 says a rejected edit "reverts to the last value Salesforce confirmed", but we never said where that value is kept. This is where.
2. **How sent outbox rows are removed:** the outbox can't use daily partitions like the inbox (T4). The "one pending row per record" index has to cover the whole table, and Postgres only enforces a unique index across partitions if it includes the partition key. So sent rows are deleted in small batches every minute instead, which keeps the delete load steady. Note that keeping sent rows for 7 days at a sustained 20 edits/s would be about 6 GB. That's the worst case, and real rates are far lower.

I also tightened one point that wasn't explicit before. A portal edit's time is taken **inside** the save transaction, after the record lock. So two portal saves to the same record always get times in the order they were actually applied.

[CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) gained three rules:
- history is append-only
- only the apply function writes `field_meta`, and it checks the shape
- there's never a second pending outbox row for a record

content.text:
I walked the brief's scenario through the tables in [data.md](docs/data.md), using the brief's own sample values. The happy path works, but the walk-through turned up eight gaps. **One is a silent wrong-winner bug.** I logged all eight as V1–V8 in [decisions.tmp.md](docs/decisions.tmp.md:293).

## The scenario, row by row

The walk-through uses a **contact**. The brief's customer fields are only name, status and owner, so a customer row has no city or phone. Both of the brief's samples are contacts, and "billing city" is already client question 11.

**Step 1: a sales user creates the contact in Salesforce.** Webhook `evt_1000`, `sequence 1`, `changedBy sales.user@client.example`.

| Table | What is written |
|---|---|
| `sync.inbox` | (`evt_1000`, today, `0031A00000Abc`, 1) |
| `contacts` | `id u-1`, `sf_id 0031A00000Abc`, `phone +91 98100 11111`, `city Mumbai`, `sf_version 1` |
| `field_meta.city` | `{updatedAt 11:00:00, source salesforce, actor ?, sfSeq 1, sfValue Mumbai}` |
| `history` | one row per field, `via webhook`, `event_id evt_1000` |

⚠️ **V4:** data.md says actor = `sf:005…`, but the brief's `changedBy` is an **email**.
⚠️ **V8:** S3 says an unknown record means "store a partial record and fetch it". But `sequence 1` already tells us this is a create carrying every field, so the fetch is wasted.

**Step 2: finance changes the city to Noida at 11:20:00.**

| Table | What is written |
|---|---|
| `contacts` | `city Noida`. `field_meta.city = {updatedAt 11:20:00, source portal, actor ?, sfSeq 1, sfValue Mumbai}` |
| `history` | city Mumbai → Noida, `via portal_save`, `change_id` **NULL** |
| `sync.outbox` | `fields {"city":"Noida"}`, `status pending`, `change_id` **NULL** until claimed |

The worker claims the row: `base_version 1`, `change_id chg_A`. It sends, and the reply says version 2. It then sets `sf_version 2` and `sfValue Noida`. The echo webhook (seq 2, `Portal_Change_Id__c chg_A`) has to look up the outbox by `change_id`.

⚠️ **V6:** that lookup has **no index**. Also, the history row was written before `change_id` existed, and history is append-only, so the row can never be linked to its send.

**Step 3: a sales user changes the phone at 11:30:04** (seq 3). `field_meta.phone.sfSeq` is 1, which is lower than 3, and 11:00 is earlier than 11:30, so the change is applied. The city stays **Noida** ✓. History answers "who changed the phone, who changed the city" ✓, once the actor is an email.

**Variant: one webhook goes missing.**

```
11:20:00  Finance saves city = Noida (outbox pending)
11:20:10  Sales sets city = Delhi    seq 2   <- webhook delayed or lost
11:20:20  Sales sets phone           seq 3   <- arrives; sf_version = 3
11:20:25  Worker sends Noida with precondition "version 3" -> Salesforce IS at 3 -> accepted
later     Gap replay brings seq 2 (Delhi): city's sfSeq is now 4 -> D19 rejects it as old
Result:   both sides say Noida. D16 says Delhi (11:20:10) should win. Wrong winner, silently.
```

## Small fixes I'll apply with your first answer (no decision needed)

| # | Fix | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| V4 | `actor` = the email from `changedBy` or `editedBy` (the portal session), with `source` saying which side | If someone's email changes later, old history keeps the old email. That's arguably correct for an audit trail |
| V5 | `sf_id` becomes `text`, unique when set, instead of `char(18)`, which pads the brief's 13-character sample IDs | None |
| V6 | Set `change_id` when the **pending row is created**. Merges keep it, and it's frozen once claimed. Add a unique index on it | Rows that are never sent still use up a key. Harmless |
| V7 | Remove `outbox.op` and decide at claim time: if `sf_id` is known, send a conditional update; otherwise an upsert on `Portal_Id__c` | None. It also covers a record edited again while its create is still in flight |
| V8 | Unknown record with seq 1: create it, no fetch. Unknown record with seq > 1: S3 (partial record plus fetch) | Without `sequence` (G3 fallback), we always fetch |

## Decision 1 of 3

❓ **V1 - Which version the precondition uses, and what to do on a `412`**

There are two problems, with one fix:
- `sf_version` is the **highest** sequence we've seen, so a gap below it lets a stale write through. That's the variant above.
- On a `412`, G1 says "GET the record and re-run D16 per field". But a GET only returns the **record's** `LastModifiedDate`, not when each field changed. So D16 can't really run per field.

- **a. Store `sf_seq_contiguous`, the highest sequence with no gap below it, and use that as the precondition. On a `412`, skip the GET:**
  1. Wait 5 s for the webhooks that are in flight.
  2. If `sf_seq_contiguous` is still behind, run a `replay_record` job to get the missing events.
  3. Re-run the guard with exact per-field `occurredAt` values, then resend.

  Our own write landing is detected when its echo arrives with our `change_id`.
  - Pros: D16 runs on the real per-field times. A missing webhook can't sneak a stale write through. The common case costs **no extra calls**.
  - Cons: one more column. A `412` delays the send by about 5–15 s, which is still inside 30 s (edit at T, first send T+1, resend about T+7 to T+16). A webhook that never arrives depends on the replay (G3 fallback: the sweep).
- **b. Keep the highest-seen version and the GET. Compare each GET value with `sfValue`:** if a field is unchanged, we still win. If it changed, use `LastModifiedDate` as its time.
  - Pros: fast, 1 call.
  - Cons: the gap bug stays. And if sales changed a *different* field after our edit, `LastModifiedDate` makes Salesforce win our field wrongly.
- **c. GET plus a replay on every `412`.**
  - Pros: exact.
  - Cons: always 2 extra calls. And it doesn't fix the precondition passing over a gap.

➡️ **a.** This changes the already-decided G1. Once you answer, I'll update data.md, then flag systems.md 2.6, CLAUDE.md rule 7, subproblem 3 and the G1 entry. V2 (a portal-created contact whose customer has no Salesforce ID yet) and V3 (no table of Salesforce users for picking an owner) come next, one at a time.

## Changes Summary

**Modified Files**

| File | Line | What changed |
|------|------|-------------|
| `docs/decisions.tmp.md` | [:293](docs/decisions.tmp.md:293) | Added Phase 5: the data.md review findings V1–V8 (three decisions, five small fixes) and the sections that must be brought in line afterwards |

**How the two sequence columns move** (V1):

| Event | `sf_seq_max` | `sf_seq_contiguous` |
|---|---|---|
| Webhook with seq = contiguous + 1 | max(max, seq) | advances to seq, then keeps advancing while the inbox already holds the next sequence |
| Webhook with seq > contiguous + 1 (a gap) | raised | unchanged. A `replay_record` job is scheduled in 10 s (D19) |
| Reply to our own write, new seq N | max(max, N) | N, if N = contiguous + 1 |
| Fetch or sweep returning the record at seq N | max(max, N) | N: a full read covers everything up to N (history for any missed events is `via fetch` / `reconcile`) |

If Salesforce sends no `sequence` (G3), both columns stay NULL and the precondition uses `sf_last_modified`.

content.text:
V1 (a) is recorded, and [data.md](docs/data.md) now includes it along with the five small fixes:

- **V1:** two columns replace `sf_version`:
  - `sf_seq_max` is the highest sequence we've seen.
  - `sf_seq_contiguous` is the highest sequence with no gap below it. The precondition uses this one.

  A new table shows how each event moves the two columns. On a `412`, the outbox row waits 5 s. If no webhook has moved `sf_seq_contiguous` past the row's `base_version` by then, a `replay_record` job runs first. There's no GET any more.
- **V4:** `actor` is the email from `changedBy` or `editedBy`. The `field_meta` example now uses the brief's own sample values.
- **V5:** every Salesforce ID column is `text`, not `char(18)`.
- **V6:** `change_id` is set when the pending outbox row is created, and has a unique index for echo lookup. History rows carry it from the moment of the save.
- **V7:** `outbox.op` is gone. Create or update is decided at claim time.
- **V8:** a jobs table now says when each job is created. A webhook with sequence 1 for an unknown record is a full create, so no fetch.

**Sections that now disagree with data.md** (I'll fix these after V3 unless you want them sooner):

| Section | What needs to change |
|---|---|
| [systems.md](docs/systems.md) 2.5 | The sample webhook uses `"Phone"` and `changedBy: "005…"`. The brief uses `"phone"` and an email |
| systems.md 2.6 | The `412` row says "GETs the record". It should say wait 5 s, then replay; the GET row should drop "after a `412`"; and the update row should say the version is `sf_seq_contiguous` |
| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) rule 7 | Says "On `412`: GET the record" |
| [subproblems.md](docs/subproblems.md) 3 | The conditional-update bullet describes the GET. It needs a new done-when check: "a missing webhook below our version gives a `412`, not a stale write" |
| [decisions.tmp.md](docs/decisions.tmp.md) G1, G2b, S3 | G1's GET step, and G2b's "a `412` whose GET shows our change ID", are replaced by V1. S3 needs V8's sequence-1 exception |
| [assumptions.md](docs/assumptions.md) 3.8 | The GET is no longer used after a `412`. The fetch should return the last modifier's **email** (V4) |

---

## Decision 2 of 3

❓ **V2 - A contact created in the portal under a customer that is also new in the portal**

Example: finance creates customer "Acme" and contact "Ravi" in the portal. Ravi's call to Salesforce needs `AccountId`, which is Acme's Salesforce ID. We don't have that until Acme's create is confirmed. The worker sends about 50 calls at once, so Ravi's call can go out while Acme's is still in flight.

- **a. Point to the customer by its External ID** (`Account.Portal_Id__c = Acme's UUID`) and let Salesforce find it.
  - Pros: no lookup on our side.
  - Cons: a new API assumption. And if Ravi's call reaches Salesforce before Acme's create lands, Salesforce replies "parent not found". We would have to retry that error instead of treating it as a rejection (D10). That's option b again, just hidden.
- **b. Hold the contact until its customer has an `sf_id`.** At claim time, if the contact's customer has no `sf_id`, push the row back by 2 s. When Acme's create reply arrives, set `customer_sf_id` on its waiting contacts, in batches of 500.
  - Pros: no new assumption, and the rule fits in one line. Ravi waits about one round trip, roughly 1 s, which is well inside 30 s.
  - Cons: the contact depends on the customer going first. If Salesforce rejects Acme, Ravi waits too. The portal shows "waiting for customer: rejected by Salesforce" until finance fixes Acme.
- **c. Send Ravi without a customer, then link him in a second call.**
  - Cons: 2 calls and an extra echo. Sales briefly sees Ravi with no account.

➡️ **b.** I first leaned towards a. Working through it showed that a still needs b's retry, so it adds an assumption for no gain.

|------|------|-------------|
| `docs/decisions.tmp.md` | [:297](docs/decisions.tmp.md:297) | Marked V1 decided, recorded the decision and rejected options, and marked V4–V8 as applied |
| `docs/data.md` | [:21](docs/data.md:21) | `sf_id` and owner columns changed to `text`. `sf_version` replaced by `sf_seq_max` and `sf_seq_contiguous` |
| | [:46](docs/data.md:46) | New table showing how the two sequence columns move |
| | [:62](docs/data.md:62) | `field_meta` example uses the brief's sample emails and values. `actor` is now defined as an email |
| | [:103](docs/data.md:103) | History `actor` is an email, and `change_id` is linked to the outbox row |
| | [:128](docs/data.md:128) | Inbox and jobs ID columns changed to `text` |
| | [:151](docs/data.md:151) | Outbox: `op` removed, `change_id` set at creation, `base_version` = `sf_seq_contiguous` |
| | [:166](docs/data.md:166) | Added the echo-lookup index, create-or-update chosen at claim time, and the wait-then-replay `412` handling |
| | [:194](docs/data.md:194) | Jobs table showing when each job is created, including V8's sequence-1 rule |

V2 (b) is recorded, and [data.md](docs/data.md) now covers it in two places:
- **4.2:** a table of the three states the two link columns can be in:
  - linked on both sides
  - "customer pending": a Salesforce contact whose customer hasn't reached us yet (D14)
  - a portal contact whose customer isn't in Salesforce yet, so its outbox row waits
- **4.5:** the rule itself. At claim time, a contact whose customer has no `sf_id` is pushed back 2 s. When the customer's create reply arrives, its contacts get `customer_sf_id`, in batches of 500, each batch its own transaction. If Salesforce rejects the customer, the contact shows "waiting for customer: rejected by Salesforce".

That adds one more section to the alignment list: the outbound path (outline item 6) has to describe the hold.

---

## Decision 3 of 3

❓ **V3 - Choosing an owner when we hold no list of Salesforce users**

The owner field holds a Salesforce user ID. Assumption 3.4 already says "portal users can only choose users synced from Salesforce", but no table in data.md holds those users. Without one, the portal can't show a list of owners, can't show an owner's name, and can't check an owner before sending.

- **a. Add a `sync.sf_users` table** (`sf_user_id`, `email`, `name`, `active`, `synced_at`).
  - The worker refreshes it every hour with one "list active users" query, at about 2,000 users per call. It also fetches any unknown owner ID that arrives in a webhook, as a job.
  - Pros: assumption 3.4 becomes true. The portal checks the owner **before** saving, so a bad owner never turns into a Salesforce rejection (D10). Owners can be shown by name.
  - Cons: a new API assumption (a users query) and one more job. It uses about 1 call an hour from the headroom, which is negligible.
- **b. No table.** The portal accepts any owner ID, Salesforce validates it, and a bad ID goes down the D10 rejection path.
  - Pros: nothing new to build or assume. The brief puts a visual interface out of scope, so names aren't strictly needed.
  - Cons: assumption 3.4 has to be rewritten. A typo becomes a round trip to Salesforce, then a revert and a "rejected" badge. History and the badge show a raw ID for the owner.
- **c. Make owner read-only in the portal.**
  - Pros: simplest.
  - Cons: the brief lists owner as a field both sides may update, so this removes something the brief requires.

➡️ **a. Described in the design, not built this weekend.** The demo seeds a few users. It isn't needed for the brief's four checks.

Once you answer, I'll add it to data.md and then bring every section on the alignment list in line in one pass: systems.md 2.5 and 2.6, CLAUDE.md rule 7, subproblem 3, the G1, G2b and S3 entries, and assumptions 3.4 and 3.8.

- **Merging:** each record has at most one pending row, and a new edit updates it. A row being sent is locked, so edits arriving meanwhile go to a new row.
- **Sending:** the worker sends to a **fake Salesforce**. Creates are upserts on `Portal_Id__c`, and every write carries `Portal_Change_Id__c`.
- **Confirmation:** the API reply is the confirmation, and it returns the record's new version.

-  - **Conditional update (G1):** every update carries the record version we last saw. A `412` leads to a GET, then the conflict rule per field, then a resend of only the winning fields. If the GET shows our own `Portal_Change_Id__c`, our earlier attempt landed.

+  - **Conditional update (G1, V1):** every update carries `sf_seq_contiguous`, the highest sequence with no gap below it. A `412` means Salesforce has events we haven't applied. The row waits 5 s for in-flight webhooks, runs a `replay_record` job if it's still behind, then re-runs the guard on exact per-field times and resends only the winning fields. There's no GET. If our earlier attempt landed, its echo arrives with our `change_id`.
+  - **Create or update at claim time (V7):** an upsert on `Portal_Id__c` if there's no `sf_id`, otherwise a conditional update. A contact whose customer has no `sf_id` waits (V2).
- **Three-step send (G2b):** claim (transaction), HTTP call (no transaction), store result (transaction). The Salesforce client throws if it is called inside `withRecordLock`.
- **Why third:** the next biggest risk is duplicates in Salesforce and loops. Every outbound feature depends on it.
- **Rules:**
- a queued older portal value doesn't overwrite a newer Salesforce value
- **a sales edit that lands in Salesforce after our guard check but before our send gets a `412`, and both sides end on the later value** (G1)
- calling the Salesforce client inside `withRecordLock` throws (G2b)
+  - **with seq 2 missing and seq 3 received, our send carries version 1 and gets a `412`, not a stale write** (V1)
+  - a contact created with its new customer is sent only after the customer's create is confirmed (V2)
## 4. Rate limiter, 429 handling, circuit breaker, surviving a restart

+- **The Salesforce users table (V3):** described in data.md 4.8. The demo seeds a few users.
- **Metrics and alerts (D24):** described in the design document (three numbers, with the red line at the brief's 30 s). Not built this weekend.
- **Initial 5M-record bulk load (D13):** assumed to run through Salesforce's bulk file API before go-live. Out of scope.

The review is finished. All three decisions and five small fixes are now in [data.md](docs/data.md), and every other doc agrees with it.

**V3 in data.md:**
- A new section, **4.8 `sync.sf_users`**: a table of Salesforce users with `sf_user_id`, `email`, `name`, `active` and `synced_at`.
  - The worker refreshes it every hour. Users who drop out are marked inactive, never deleted, because old records still point at them.
  - An owner ID we don't recognise triggers a `fetch_user` job.
  - The portal checks a new owner against active users before saving, so a bad owner becomes a `400` in the portal instead of a Salesforce rejection.
  - Marked "described, not built this weekend".
- The overview, the jobs table and the role table include it. The old 4.8 and 4.9 are now 4.9 and 4.10.

**Brought in line with data.md:**

| Doc | Change |
|---|---|
| [systems.md](docs/systems.md) | **2.3:** lists `sync.sf_users` and links to data.md. **2.5:** the sample webhook uses the brief's values (`phone`, an email for `changedBy`), plus notes on field names and the sequence-1 create rule (V8). **2.6:** upsert vs update decided at claim time, plus the contact hold (V7, V2). The update now sends `sf_seq_contiguous` as its version (V1). The GET is no longer used after a `412`. New "list active users" call. The `412` row now waits, then replays (V1). The send's claim step reads `sf_seq_contiguous` |
| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) | Rule 7 rewritten for V1. New rule 9: never send a contact before its customer has a Salesforce ID |
| [subproblems.md](docs/subproblems.md) | Subproblem 3: V1 and V7 bullets, and two new done-when checks (a missing seq 2 gives a `412`; a contact goes only after its customer is confirmed). The users table is listed as not built |

content.text:
## What the inbound path is

The **inbound path** is everything that happens when **Salesforce tells us something changed**. It runs from the moment the webhook hits our endpoint until the change is safely in Postgres and we reply `200`. It's the opposite direction from the outbound path (item 6), which goes from a portal edit to a Salesforce API call.

```
Sales user edits in Salesforce
        |
        v
Salesforce --HTTPS webhook--> Load balancer --> Webhook receiver --> Postgres
                                                     |
                                         one transaction, then 200
```

Only the receiver is involved. It **never calls Salesforce**. If it needs something from Salesforce, it leaves a job row for the worker.

## The steps, in order

| # | Step | If it fails | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Check `X-Timestamp` is within 5 minutes and that the HMAC signature matches | `401`, nothing stored | D7 |
| 2 | Check the body has `eventId`, `recordId`, a known `objectType`, `sequence`, `occurredAt` | `400`, nothing stored | S2 |
| 3 | `BEGIN`, then insert the keys into `sync.inbox` | Already there → duplicate → `200`, stop | D18 |
| 4 | Find the record by `sf_id` and lock its row | Unknown: seq 1 → create it; seq > 1 → store what we have, plus a `fetch_record` job | G2, S3, V8 |
| 5 | Our own echo? `Portal_Change_Id__c` matches an outbox `change_id` | Mark the outbox row confirmed; no duplicate history row | D17 |
| 6 | For each field: is this event's `sequence` newer than the field's `sfSeq`? | No → don't apply; history row marked superseded | D19 |
| 7 | For each field: is `occurredAt` later than the field's `updatedAt`? | No → the portal value stays; history row marked superseded | D16 |
| 8 | Write the values, `field_meta`, `sf_seq_max` and `sf_seq_contiguous`, history rows, and any jobs (gap, missing customer) | — | data.md |
| 9 | `COMMIT`, then reply `200` | Crash before the commit → no `200` → Salesforce retries. Database down → `503` | D12 |

## A worked example: the brief's own sample

**The contact before the webhook**, after finance changed the city:

| Column | Value |
|---|---|
| `sf_id` | `0031A00000Abc` |
| `phone` | `+91 98100 11111`, `field_meta.phone = {updatedAt 11:00:00, source salesforce, actor sales.user@…, sfSeq 1}` |
| `city` | `Noida`, `field_meta.city = {updatedAt 11:20:00, source portal, actor finance.user@…, sfSeq 2}` |
| `sf_seq_max` / `sf_seq_contiguous` | 2 / 2 |

**The webhook arrives** (the brief's sample, plus our `sequence`):

```json
{ "eventId": "evt_1001", "recordId": "0031A00000Abc", "objectType": "Contact",
  "sequence": 3, "occurredAt": "2026-11-02T11:30:04.000Z",
  "changedBy": "sales.user@client.example",
  "changedFields": { "phone": "+919876543210" } }
```

**What the receiver does:**
1. The signature and timestamp check out.
2. The body is complete.
3. `INSERT INTO sync.inbox (evt_1001, today, 0031A00000Abc, 3)` inserts 1 row, so this isn't a duplicate.
4. It finds the contact by `sf_id` and locks it.
5. There's no `Portal_Change_Id__c`, so this isn't our echo.
6. Phone: sequence 3 is higher than the field's `sfSeq` of 1 ✓.
7. Phone: 11:30:04 is later than 11:00:00 ✓, so the change is applied.
8. It writes `phone = +919876543210` and `field_meta.phone = {updatedAt 11:30:04, source salesforce, actor sales.user@client.example, sfSeq 3, sfValue +919876543210}`. Both sequence columns become 3, since 3 = 2 + 1. History gets one row: phone, old `+91 98100 11111` → new `+919876543210`, `via webhook`, `event_id evt_1001`, `superseded false`.
9. `COMMIT`, then `200`.

**Result:** the new phone, and the city is still finance's **Noida**, because the webhook never touched it. History can answer both "who changed the phone" (sales.user) and "who changed the city" (finance.user). That's the brief's whole scenario.

## The same webhook in the other cases

| What happens next | Where it stops | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `evt_1001` is delivered **again** | Step 3: the inbox already has it | `200`, nothing changes |
| An **older** event (seq 2, an old phone) arrives **after** seq 3 | Step 6: 2 is not higher than the phone's `sfSeq` of 3 | Phone stays; the old value goes to history as superseded |
| **Seq 5** arrives while seq 4 is missing | Step 8: 5 is above 3 + 1 | Seq 5 is applied, `sf_seq_contiguous` stays at 3, and a `replay_record` job runs in 10 s |
| The webhook is **our own** city write coming back | Step 5: its `change_id` matches | The outbox row is confirmed, and nothing is sent back (loop rule) |
| A **new** contact, seq 1, whose customer we don't have | Step 4 creates it; step 8 adds a `fetch_customer` job | Shown as "customer pending" until the customer arrives |

All the rules this uses are already decided, so most of item 5 is writing up what we have. Before writing it, I'd check for open questions. One candidate is the order of step 5 (echo) against steps 6–7: an echo can arrive after a newer sales edit to the same field.

I checked the inbound path against every decision so far. **One question needs your input.** The other five points are clarifications I'll just write in. Everything is logged as Phase 6 in [decisions.tmp.md](docs/decisions.tmp.md:347).

## Clarifications (no decision needed)

- **Fields we don't sync** (e.g. `Description`) are ignored and logged. The brief says "these fields and no others".
- **A changed `AccountId`** moves the contact to the new customer. If we don't have that customer yet, a `fetch_customer` job is added.
- **The same event delivered twice at the same moment:** the second insert into the inbox waits for the first to commit, then does nothing and returns `200`.
- **Replay, fetch and sweep results** go through the same steps 3–9, run by the worker, with `via = replay / fetch / reconcile`. Only steps 1–2 (signature and body checks) belong to the receiver alone.
- **Time budget:** one transaction of a few milliseconds. If the record lock can't be had within 2 s, we return `503` and Salesforce retries.

---

❓ **I1 - Applying our own echo when a newer sales edit got there first**

D17 only says an echo should "record its sequence, no duplicate history row". It doesn't say what happens to the field. Here's the case that matters:

```
11:20:00  Finance saves city = Noida; worker sends it; Salesforce applies it as seq 4
11:20:30  Sales sets city = Delhi                     seq 5
          Webhooks arrive in the other order:
11:20:31  seq 5 (Delhi) -> applied: city = Delhi, field_meta.city.sfSeq = 5
11:20:32  seq 4 echo (Noida, our change_id, changedBy = integration user)
```

If the echo were applied like any other event, two things would go wrong:
- **Who changed the field** would become the integration user, so the field would no longer say finance set the city. That matters if the echo is the latest event, which is the usual case.
- **`sfValue`**, the value Salesforce holds, could be set to Noida even though Salesforce holds Delhi. A later rejection (D10) would then revert to the wrong value.

The worker's `2xx` reply has the same risk if it arrives after the seq 5 webhook.

- **a. An echo goes through the normal per-field checks, with three exceptions:**
  1. The outbox row is marked confirmed, whatever happens to the fields.
  2. For a field where Salesforce kept **exactly what we sent**: move `sfSeq` and `sfValue` forward **only if this sequence is newer**. Keep the portal save's `updatedAt`, source and actor. Write no history row, because the portal save already wrote one.
  3. For a field where Salesforce **changed** our value (e.g. reformatted the phone): apply it as a Salesforce change, noted "normalised by Salesforce" (D17). It's never sent back.

  The worker's `2xx` reply follows the same "only move forward" rule.

  In the case above, the late echo finds city at `sfSeq 5`, so it changes nothing about the field. The outbox row is confirmed, and Delhi stays with its own actor.
  - Pros: a late echo or reply can't drag anything backwards. The field keeps finance as the person who set it. `sfValue` is always what Salesforce really holds. Salesforce's reformatting still reaches the portal.
  - Cons: three more branches in the apply function. It's a plain function with no I/O, so each branch is a millisecond unit test.
- **b. An echo only updates the record's sequence columns and confirms the outbox row. It never touches fields.**
  - Pros: simplest.
  - Cons: Salesforce's reformatting is lost, which breaks D17's "normalised by Salesforce" rule. `sfValue` then relies only on the reply, and the late-reply risk stays.
- **c. Treat an echo as a completely normal event.**
  - Cons: the integration user replaces finance as the person who set the field, and only history still shows finance. That works against the brief's "who changed the city".

➡️ **a.** Once you answer, I'll write the inbound section, the step table plus the worked example and branches from last turn, as `docs/inbound.md`, and flag anything else that needs to match it. D17's entry and the outbound reply handling are likely candidates.

| File | Line | What changed |
|------|------|-------------|
| `docs/decisions.tmp.md` | [:347](docs/decisions.tmp.md:347) | Added Phase 6 (inbound path): open question I1 on how a late echo is applied, and five clarifications |

input.content:
# 5. The inbound path, from webhook to our database

The inbound path is everything that happens when **Salesforce tells us a record changed**. It starts when
the webhook reaches our endpoint and ends when the change is committed in Postgres and we reply `200`.
Table and column names are defined in [data.md](data.md). Labels like `D18` point to
[decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md).

```
Sales user edits in Salesforce
        |
        v
Salesforce --HTTPS POST /webhooks/salesforce--> Load balancer (TLS) --> Webhook receiver --> Postgres
                                                                         one transaction, then 200
```

Only the **webhook receiver** takes part. It never calls Salesforce (D22). When it needs something from
Salesforce, such as a missing customer or a missing event, it writes a row to `sync.jobs` for the worker.

## 5.1 The steps

| # | Step | Outcome if it stops here | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Check `X-Timestamp` is within 5 minutes and that `X-Signature` is the HMAC-SHA256 of timestamp + body | `401`, nothing stored, Salesforce doesn't retry | D7 |
| 2 | Check the body has `eventId`, `recordId`, a known `objectType`, `sequence`, `occurredAt`, `changedBy` and `changedFields` | `400`, nothing stored, logged and counted in M3 | S2 |
| 3 | `BEGIN`. `INSERT INTO sync.inbox (event_id, received_day, record_id, sequence) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` | 0 rows inserted means a duplicate: `COMMIT`, `200`, stop | D18, T4 |
| 4 | Find the record by `sf_id` and lock its row (`withRecordLock`). If it's unknown, see 5.3 | – | G2, S3, V8 |
| 5 | Is it **our own echo**? Does `changedFields.Portal_Change_Id__c` match an outbox `change_id`? | Mark that outbox row confirmed, and use the echo rules in 5.2 | D17, I1 |
| 6–7 | For **each field**, run the apply rule in 5.2: sequence first, then time | – | D19, D16 |
| 8 | Write values, `field_meta`, `sf_seq_max`, `sf_seq_contiguous`, history rows, and any jobs (5.4) | – | data.md |
| 9 | `COMMIT`, then reply `200` | Crash before the commit means no `200`, and Salesforce retries. Database down, or a lock wait over 2 s, gives `503` and Salesforce retries | D12, G2b |

Everything from step 3 to step 9 is **one transaction**. A `200` always means the change and its history are
on disk.

```
handleWebhook(req):
  verifySignature(req)                      -> 401
  event = parseAndValidate(req.body)        -> 400
  withTransaction:
    if not insertInbox(event): return 200   -- duplicate
    withRecordLock(event.recordId):         -- creates the row first if unknown (5.3)
      state   = loadRecord(event.recordId)
      echoRow = findOutboxByChangeId(event.changedFields.Portal_Change_Id__c)
      result  = applyEvent(state, event, echoRow)    -- pure function, no I/O (subproblem 2)
      write(result.record, result.historyRows, result.jobs, result.outboxConfirm)
  return 200
```

## 5.2 The apply rule, field by field

`applyEvent` looks at each key in `changedFields` against that field's `field_meta`. The first matching row
decides.

| # | Condition | Field value and `updatedAt` / `source` / `actor` | `sfSeq` / `sfValue` | History row |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a | Not a field we sync (e.g. `Description`) | unchanged; logged | unchanged | none |
| b | `event.sequence <= sfSeq` (an **older or repeated** event, D19) | unchanged | unchanged | yes, `superseded = true` |
| c | **Echo**, and the value is exactly what we sent (I1) | **unchanged**: the field keeps the portal save's time and actor | set to this sequence and value | none: the portal save already wrote one |
| d | **Echo**, but Salesforce changed our value, e.g. reformatted a phone (I1, D17) | applied as a Salesforce change | set | yes, note "normalised by Salesforce" |
| e | `occurredAt < updatedAt`: the portal value is **newer** (D16) | unchanged: the portal value stays and its outbox row will send it | set: Salesforce does hold this value right now | yes, `superseded = true` |
| f | Otherwise, including an exact time tie, which Salesforce wins (D16) | value = new value, `updatedAt = occurredAt`, `source = salesforce`, `actor = changedBy` | set | yes, `superseded = false` |

- **Sequence before time.** Row b runs before rows e and f. An older event can never win on time, even
  with a skewed clock.
- **"Set" always means "move forward only".** `sfSeq` and `sfValue` change only when this event's sequence is
  higher than the stored one. The worker's `2xx` reply follows the same rule, so neither a late echo nor a
  late reply can move anything backwards (I1).
- **Other fields in the same event** are judged separately. An old event's change to a field nobody has
  touched since still lands (D19).
- **The `Portal_Id__c` and `Portal_Change_Id__c` keys** are used only to recognise an echo. They aren't
  stored as fields.

## 5.3 A record we don't have yet

| Case | What happens |
|---|---|
| Unknown `recordId`, `sequence = 1` | A **create** carrying every field. Insert the row with a new UUID `id` and `sf_id = recordId`, then apply the rule. No fetch is needed (V8) |
| Unknown `recordId`, `sequence > 1` | We've missed the create. Insert a row holding only the fields received, and add a `fetch_record` job at 5 s, 15 s and 25 s (S3). The fetch stamps fields with the record's sequence (`via = fetch`) |
| A contact whose `customer` (`AccountId`) we don't have | Store `customer_sf_id` and leave `customer_id` NULL, shown as "customer pending". Add a `fetch_customer` job (D14) |
| A contact whose `customer` **changed** | Relink `customer_id` to the new customer, or mark it pending and fetch the customer as above |
| A customer arrives that waiting contacts point at | Link its pending contacts (`customer_sf_id` matches) in batches of 500, each its own transaction (G2b) |

## 5.4 Record-level updates and jobs

| After applying the fields | Effect |
|---|---|
| `sequence = sf_seq_contiguous + 1` | `sf_seq_contiguous` advances, then keeps advancing while the inbox already holds the next sequence. `sf_seq_max` is raised |
| `sequence > sf_seq_contiguous + 1` (a **gap**) | `sf_seq_max` is raised, and `sf_seq_contiguous` stays. A `replay_record` job runs in 10 s if the gap is still open (D19). Any outbox send for this record meanwhile gets a `412`, never a stale write (V1) |
| An echo | Also sets the outbox row to confirmed (`sent`), whatever happened to the fields |
| An owner ID not in `sync.sf_users` | A `fetch_user` job (V3) |

## 5.5 Worked example: the brief's sample webhook

**Before.** Finance has changed the city:

| Column | Value |
|---|---|
| `sf_id` | `0031A00000Abc` |
| `phone` | `+91 98100 11111`. `field_meta.phone = {updatedAt 11:00:00, source salesforce, actor sales.user@client.example, sfSeq 1, sfValue +91 98100 11111}` |
| `city` | `Noida`. `field_meta.city = {updatedAt 11:20:00, source portal, actor finance.user@client.example, sfSeq 2, sfValue Noida}` |
| `sf_seq_max` / `sf_seq_contiguous` | 2 / 2 |

**Webhook** (the brief's sample, plus `sequence`):

```json
{ "eventId": "evt_1001", "recordId": "0031A00000Abc", "objectType": "Contact",
  "sequence": 3, "occurredAt": "2026-11-02T11:30:04.000Z",
  "changedBy": "sales.user@client.example",
  "changedFields": { "phone": "+919876543210" } }
```

**Steps:**
1–2. The signature and body are valid.
3. Inbox row (`evt_1001`, today, `0031A00000Abc`, 3) is inserted, so it isn't a duplicate.
4. The contact is found by `sf_id` and locked.
5. There's no `Portal_Change_Id__c`, so it isn't an echo.
6–7. Phone: 3 is above `sfSeq` 1, and 11:30:04 is later than 11:00:00, so row f applies.
8. `phone = +919876543210` and `field_meta.phone = {updatedAt 11:30:04, source salesforce, actor sales.user@client.example, sfSeq 3, sfValue +919876543210}`. Both sequence columns become 3. One history row: phone `+91 98100 11111` → `+919876543210`, `via webhook`, `event_id evt_1001`, `superseded false`.
9. `COMMIT`, then `200`.

**After:** the new phone, with the city still **Noida** from finance. History answers both "who changed the
phone" (sales.user) and "who changed the city" (finance.user). This is the brief's scenario.

## 5.6 The same path in the other cases

| What arrives | Where it's decided | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `evt_1001` **again** | Step 3 | `200`. Nothing changes |
| `evt_1001` again on a **later day** (the inbox partition has rolled over) | Row b | The phone isn't touched. One extra history row marked superseded (T4) |
| An **older** event, seq 2 with an old phone, after seq 3 | Row b | The phone stays. The old value goes to history as superseded |
| **Seq 5** while seq 4 is missing | 5.4 gap | Seq 5 is applied. `sf_seq_contiguous` stays at 3, and `replay_record` runs in 10 s |
| **Our own** city write coming back (seq 4, Noida) | Row c | The outbox row is confirmed. The field keeps finance as the actor, and there's no history row. **Nothing is sent back** (D17) |
| Our echo arriving **after** a newer sales edit (seq 5, Delhi) | Rows b/c | City stays Delhi with its own actor. The echo only confirms the outbox row (I1) |
| Salesforce reformatted the phone we sent | Row d | The reformatted phone is applied, noted "normalised by Salesforce", and never sent back |
| Sales sets the city at 11:19:59, the webhook arrives after finance's 11:20:00 save | Row e | Portal keeps Noida. `sfValue` becomes Salesforce's value. The pending outbox row sends Noida with a precondition (G1) |
| A **new** contact (seq 1) whose customer we don't have | 5.3 | Created and shown "customer pending". `fetch_customer` runs |

## 5.7 Who else uses this path

The worker runs **steps 3–9** (the same `applyEvent`) for events it gets from Salesforce itself:

| Source | `via` | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Change-log replay, after an outage or for a gap (G4, D19) | `replay` | Each event also goes into the inbox, so the overlap with webhooks we already have is dropped |
| Single-record fetch (D14, S3) | `fetch` | One "event" carrying the record's current sequence and every field |
| Reconciliation sweep (G3) | `reconcile` | Only fields that are newer and different get written |

Steps 1–2 (signature and body checks) belong to the receiver alone.

## 5.8 Where the brief's required rules live on this path

| Brief | Here |
|---|---|
| A duplicate webhook | Step 3 (inbox), backed up by row b |
| An older webhook after a newer one | Row b (per-field `sequence`), plus the 5.4 gap replay |
| Our own update coming back (sync loop) | Rows c and d. The webhook path **never writes to the outbox** (D17) |
| Webhooks lost during the 6-hour outage | 5.7 replay from the heartbeat minus 10 minutes (G4) |

[decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md).

```

        |
        v
Salesforce --HTTPS POST /webhooks/salesforce--> Load balancer (TLS) --> Webhook receiver --> Postgres
                                                                         one transaction, then 200
```

Salesforce, such as a missing customer or a missing event, it writes a row to `sync.jobs` for the worker.

| 1 | Check `X-Timestamp` is within 5 minutes and that `X-Signature` is the HMAC-SHA256 of timestamp + body | `401`, nothing stored, Salesforce doesn't retry | D7 |
| 2 | Check the body has `eventId`, `recordId`, a known `objectType`, `sequence`, `occurredAt`, `changedBy` and `changedFields` | `400`, nothing stored, logged and counted in M3 | S2 |
| 3 | `BEGIN`. `INSERT INTO sync.inbox (event_id, received_day, record_id, sequence) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` | 0 rows inserted means a duplicate: `COMMIT`, `200`, stop | D18, T4 |
| 4 | Find the record by `sf_id` and lock its row (`withRecordLock`). If it's unknown, see 5.3 | – | G2, S3, V8 |
| 5 | Is it **our own echo**? Does `changedFields.Portal_Change_Id__c` match an outbox `change_id`? | Mark that outbox row confirmed, and use the echo rules in 5.2 | D17, I1 |

| 8 | Write values, `field_meta`, `sf_seq_max`, `sf_seq_contiguous`, history rows, and any jobs (5.4) | – | data.md |

# Tequity Round 1 - Salesforce <-> portal sync

Design docs live in `docs/`: decisions in `decisions.tmp.md`, assumptions in `assumptions.md`,
build order in `subproblems.md`. Decision labels (`Dn`, `Sn`) point into `decisions.tmp.md`.

## Shared database and `saveEdit()` module (decision S4) - keep these rules when changing code

The portal backend, the webhook receiver and the sync worker share one Postgres database. A portal
edit writes the record, its history and the outbox row in **one transaction** through a shared
`saveEdit()` module. That transaction is what stops a crash from losing an edit or sending an
unsaved one (D23). The costs we accepted, and the rules that contain them:

1. **Every portal write goes through `saveEdit()`.** A direct `UPDATE` on a records table skips the
   outbox, and that edit silently never reaches Salesforce. A test must fail if a record row changes
   without a matching outbox row. Never bypass it, even for scripts or admin fixes.
2. **The webhook path never writes to the outbox** (loop rule, D17). Do not add a database trigger
   that writes the outbox on every update: it would also fire on webhook writes.
3. **Sync tables live in their own `sync` schema** (`inbox`, `outbox`, `jobs`). The sync code owns
   their migrations; the portal only calls the module.
4. **Same language:** the module is TypeScript on Node (20+), the portal backend's language.
5. **Each service has its own capped connection pool** (e.g. receiver 10, worker 5), so a webhook
   burst or an outage drain cannot starve portal users.
6. **A failed outbox insert fails the user's save.** This is deliberate: a save that cannot be
   synced must not look saved.
7. **One Postgres role per service, least privilege.** For example, the receiver cannot touch
   `outbox`; the worker never receives HTTP; the receiver never calls Salesforce (D22).

## Locking and the Salesforce precondition (decisions G1, G2, G2b) - keep these rules

1. **Every write to per-field state goes through `withRecordLock(recordId, fn)`**: lock the record row
   (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), read, run the pure apply function, write, commit. No other way to open a
   transaction on records.
2. **Never call Salesforce inside a transaction.** The Salesforce client throws when called inside
   `withRecordLock`; keep that check and its test. The worker sends in three steps: claim (tx) -> HTTP
   call (no tx) -> store result (tx).
3. **Lock order:** customer before contact, then by ID. Deadlock victims retry.
4. **One record per transaction** for replay, drain and sweep. Bulk work (e.g. linking contacts to a
   newly arrived customer) runs in batches of 500, each its own transaction.
5. **Keep transactions to database writes only.** Emails, HTTP calls and other side effects happen
   after the commit.
6. **Postgres timeouts per role:** `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 5s`, `lock_timeout = 2s`,
   `statement_timeout = 5s`. Migrations use their own role with a `lock_timeout`.
7. **Every update to Salesforce is conditional on `sf_seq_contiguous`** (the highest sequence with no
   gap below it), never on `sf_seq_max`: a missing webhook below our version must cause a `412`, not a
   stale write. On `412`: no GET. Wait 5 s for in-flight webhooks; if `sf_seq_contiguous` has not
   passed `base_version`, run a `replay_record` job; then re-run the guard on exact per-field times and
   resend only the winners. Our own landed write is recognised by its echo's `change_id`. Never retry a
   lost field automatically; the user overrides with "Use my value again".
8. **Replay restarts from a heartbeat minus an overlap**, never from "the last `eventId` we applied"
   (webhooks arrive out of order).
9. **A contact is never sent before its customer has an `sf_id`**; the claim pushes it back 2 s.

## Other fixed rules

- Only one sync worker is active at a time (Postgres advisory lock, standby takes over). The rate
  limiter is in memory; do not scale the worker horizontally without a shared limiter.
- Contact full name is stored as `first_name` / `last_name` (Salesforce `Contact.Name` is read-only).
- **`history` is append-only:** insert, never update or delete (old partitions are archived, not
  deleted). `superseded` is set at insert time by the apply rule.
- **`field_meta` (JSONB) has no database-enforced shape:** only the apply function writes it, and it
  validates `{updatedAt, source, actor, sfSeq, sfValue}` for every field. Table layouts are in
  `docs/data.md`.
- **At most one pending outbox row per record**, enforced by a unique partial index; merge with
  `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`, never a second pending row.

content.text:
I1 (a) is recorded, and outline item 5 is written as [docs/inbound.md](docs/inbound.md).

**What the section covers:**
- **5.1 The steps:** the nine steps with what happens if each one stops the webhook (`401` / `400` / duplicate `200` / `503`), plus a short pseudocode version. Steps 3–9 are one transaction, so a `200` always means the change and its history are on disk.
- **5.2 The apply rule, field by field:** checked in order, echo first, then sequence, then time:
  - a: a field we don't sync is ignored
  - b: an echo kept as sent
  - c: an echo Salesforce reformatted
  - d: an older or repeated event
  - e: the portal value is newer
  - f: apply the change

  `sfSeq` and `sfValue` only ever move forward.
- **5.3 A record we don't have yet:** a create (seq 1), a missed create (seq > 1, so fetch), a contact whose customer is missing, a contact moving to another customer, and linking waiting contacts.
- **5.4 Record-level updates:** the two sequence columns, gap replay, confirming the echo's outbox row, and an unknown owner.
- **5.5 Worked example:** the brief's sample webhook, row by row.
- **5.6 Nine other cases:** a duplicate, a duplicate on a later day, an older event, a gap, our echo, a late echo, a reformatted value, a newer portal value, a new contact.
- **5.7 Reuse:** replay, fetch and the sweep go through the same steps 3–9.
- **5.8 The brief's required rules:** where each one lives on this path.

**One fix while writing:** my first draft checked the older-event rule before the echo rule. That would have made a late echo write a history row, against I1. Echo rows now come first.

**One rule I made explicit:** when a Salesforce value loses to a newer portal value (row e), `sfSeq` and `sfValue` still move forward, because Salesforce really does hold that value until our pending write lands. That keeps D10's revert pointing at the right value.

**Brought in line with inbound.md:**
- [data.md](docs/data.md): the reply-to-our-write row, and the `sfValue` definition.
- [systems.md](docs/systems.md): the `2xx` reply row now only moves values forward.
- [subproblems.md](docs/subproblems.md): two new tests for late echoes in subproblem 2, and the loop bullet in subproblem 3.
- [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md): a new "`sfSeq` and `sfValue` only move forward" rule.
- D17's entry in [decisions.tmp.md](docs/decisions.tmp.md:481) is marked "made precise by I1".

content.text:
**The current rules don't guarantee one contact. Your scenario ends with two.** D9 and assumption 3.3 already said "match the create's webhook by `Portal_Id__c`", but §5.1 and §5.3 never implemented it. I've logged this as I2 in [decisions.tmp.md](docs/decisions.tmp.md:383).

## Walk-through with the rules as written

**Starting state:**

| Table | Row |
|---|---|
| `contacts` | `id u-1`, `sf_id NULL`, Ravi Kumar, … |
| `sync.outbox` | `r1`: `record_id u-1`, `change_id chg_A`, `status pending` |

**T0: the worker claims r1.** There's no `sf_id`, so it sends an **upsert on `Portal_Id__c = u-1`** (V7) and sets r1 to `sending`. Salesforce creates `0031A00000Xyz` (seq 1), but the reply is lost. After the 10 s timeout, r1 stays `sending`, to be resent after 60 s (G2b).

**T0 + 1 s: the create webhook arrives:**

```json
{ "eventId": "evt_2001", "recordId": "0031A00000Xyz", "objectType": "Contact", "sequence": 1,
  "changedBy": "integration@client.example",
  "changedFields": { "firstName": "Ravi", "lastName": "Kumar", ...,
                     "Portal_Id__c": "u-1", "Portal_Change_Id__c": "chg_A" } }
```

| Step | What happens today |
|---|---|
| 3 | The inbox insert succeeds, so it isn't a duplicate |
| **4** | **Looks up `sf_id = 0031A00000Xyz`. Not found**, because `u-1.sf_id` is still NULL |
| **5.3** | Unknown record with seq 1, so it **inserts a new row `u-2`** with `sf_id 0031A00000Xyz` |
| 5 | `chg_A` matches r1, so **r1 is marked `sent`** |

**Result:**

| Row | State |
|---|---|
| `u-1` | `sf_id NULL` forever. r1 is `sent`, so the worker never resends, and the lost reply never comes back |
| `u-2` | The real Salesforce link |

The portal shows **two Ravis**. Worse, a later edit to `u-1` goes out as an upsert on `Portal_Id__c = u-1`. Salesforce applies it to `0031A00000Xyz`, and the echo then updates **`u-2`**. Two portal rows end up driving one Salesforce record.

**And it depends on timing:** if the worker's 60 s resend gets there before the webhook, the upsert finds the existing record, the reply sets `u-1.sf_id`, and the webhook then finds `u-1`. So sometimes we get one row and sometimes two.

The unique index on `sf_id` doesn't help, because `u-1`'s `sf_id` is NULL. The most it could do is make the worker's late reply **fail** when it tries to give `u-1` an ID that `u-2` already has.

---

❓ **I2 - The lookup order for a webhook whose `recordId` we don't recognise**

- **a. Look up in this order: `sf_id` → `Portal_Id__c` → create.**
  1. Look up by `sf_id = recordId`.
  2. Not found, and `changedFields` has `Portal_Id__c`: look up **`id = Portal_Id__c`** and lock that row. If its `sf_id` is NULL, **adopt it**: set `sf_id = recordId` on it.
  3. Still not found: seq 1 creates a row (with `id = Portal_Id__c` if present, else a new UUID), and seq > 1 does S3 (partial record plus fetch).

  Then the event carries on as normal. Here it's our echo, so r1 is confirmed `sent`. The fields were kept as sent, so there are no history rows and the portal actor stays (I1). Both sequence columns become 1.

  The worker's late reply or its resend locks the same `u-1` row. It finds `sf_id` already equal to `0031A00000Xyz`, which is the same value, so there's no conflict. A resent upsert lands on the existing record by External ID, so there's still no duplicate in Salesforce.

  If `Portal_Id__c` points at a row that already holds a **different** `sf_id`, that would mean Salesforce has two records with our External ID. Assumption 3.2 makes the External ID unique, so this shouldn't happen. If it does, we don't apply the event, we log it, and we count it toward M3.
  - Pros: exactly one row whatever the timing. Uses data the webhook already carries. One primary-key lookup, and only when the `sf_id` lookup misses.
  - Cons: one more branch in step 4. It relies on `Portal_Id__c` being in `changedFields` on our creates, which D8 already assumes.
- **b. When `sf_id` is unknown and `Portal_Id__c` is present, park the webhook as a job until the worker's resend sets `sf_id`, then apply it.**
  - Pros: only the worker ever assigns an `sf_id`.
  - Cons: the create shows up in the portal 60 s or more late, past the 30 s target. More moving parts.
- **c. Allow the duplicate, and merge `u-2` into `u-1` with a clean-up job.**
  - Cons: the duplicate is visible, and the merge has to move history, contacts and outbox rows. That's exactly the kind of messy repair the design avoids.

➡️ **a.** Once you answer, I'll update inbound.md step 4 and §5.3 with this lookup order, add this scenario to the §5.6 table, and flag what else has to match: the worker's handling of the create reply in item 6, and a done-when check in subproblem 3.

## Changes Summary

**Modified Files**

| File | Line | What changed |
|------|------|-------------|
| `docs/decisions.tmp.md` | [:383](docs/decisions.tmp.md:383) | Added I2 (OPEN): the duplicate-contact bug when a create reply is lost, and why the outcome depends on timing |

message.content: Yes, option a
