| **Our restarts** | Nothing is lost: every pending call is a row in Postgres, and a `sending` row is picked up again when its lease has expired (outbound.md 6.3) |
| **Alert** | The breaker open for more than 5 minutes pages (D24) |

## 10.2 What is on disk after 6 hours

Worst case: the portal peak of **20 edits/s** lasts the full 6 h, and no two edits touch the same record, so
nothing merges.

| Where | Rows | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `sync.outbox` (pending, plus at most one `sending` row per record) | 20 × 21,600 = **432,000** | × ~500 B ≈ **216 MB** |
| `history`, one row per portal edit (already counted in the history budget, D15) | 432,000 | × ~200 B ≈ 86 MB |
| `sync.inbox`, only for webhooks that did arrive | up to 30 × 21,600 = 648,000 | × ~150 B ≈ 97 MB |
| `sync.watermarks` | the sweep's last successful point (the replay start) | tiny |

Everything is in Postgres, written in the same transaction as the edit, so it survives any restart of our
processes. With merging, the outbox holds one row per edited record instead of one per edit.

## 10.3 Recovery order

1. **The breaker closes** on a successful test call.
2. **Replay Salesforce's change log first** (D3, D21), for the whole window in which webhooks may have been lost.
   **Proposed start point (Q10a, pending):** the sweep's watermark minus 10 minutes. The sweep runs every 5
   minutes, so its watermark is at most 5 minutes before the outage began, even in a quiet hour when nothing
   else would have noticed the outage. Each replayed event goes through the inbox and the normal apply rule
   (`via replay`), so events we already have are dropped.
3. **Drain the outbox** with a ramp of **20 → 40 → 80 req/s** (minute 1, minute 2, then on), in two lanes:
   **fresh** rows (created after recovery) and **backlog** rows, 50/50, each lane borrowing the other's unused
   share (D21).
4. The sweep resumes and catches anything the replay couldn't return.

**Why replay first:** a queued 10:00 finance value must not overwrite an 11:00 sales edit from the outage. With
the replay applied first, the sales value's `editId` has replaced finance's, so the guard drops the stale field
before any call. The conditional update would also catch it (`412`), so replay-first is no longer what makes
this correct; it's what avoids hundreds of thousands of `412`s at the start of the drain (V1).

## 10.4 The arithmetic

**Inputs**

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Outage | 6 h = 21,600 s | brief |
| Portal edits at peak | 20/s, for the whole outage and the drain | assumption 1.1 |
| Salesforce edits at peak | 30/s | assumption 1.1 |
| Send rate | 80 req/s; 20 req/s of the 100 cap stays free for retries, `412` evidence, fetches and gap replays | assumption 3.1 |
| Ramp | 20 req/s in minute 1, 40 in minute 2, then 80 | D11 |
| Replay page | 2,000 events per call | assumption 1.3 |

**Backlog:** 20 edits/s × 21,600 s = **432,000 calls**.

**Replay:** the window is the outage plus up to 15 minutes before it (up to 5 minutes of sweep staleness plus the
10-minute overlap): 30 events/s × (21,600 + 900) s = 675,000 events, and 675,000 ÷ 2,000 = **338 calls**.

**Drain.** Find the time T, in seconds after recovery, when everything sent equals everything needed:

```
sent(T)   = 20 x 60  +  40 x 60  +  80 x (T - 120)  =  80T - 6,000      (ramp, then 80 req/s)
needed(T) = 432,000  +  338  +  20T                                      (backlog + replay + new portal edits)

80T - 6,000 = 432,338 + 20T
        60T = 438,338
          T = 438,338 / 60 = 7,305.6 s
          T = 7,305.6 / 60 = 121.8 min   ~ 122 minutes
```

**If half the outage edits hit a record already queued** (a guess; the real ratio is client question 9): the
backlog is 216,000 calls, so 60T = 216,000 + 338 + 6,000 = 222,338, and T = 222,338 ÷ 60 = 3,705.6 s ≈ **62
minutes**.

**The order doesn't change the time.** The total to send and the rate are fixed, so the lanes decide only *which*
calls wait, not how long the drain takes. Per lane after the ramp: fresh edits arrive at 20/s against a 40/s lane,
so they go out within about a second; the backlog gets the remaining 60/s and still finishes at about 122
minutes. During the 2-minute ramp, fresh edits can wait longer than 30 s; that's inside the catch-up period, which
the brief treats as a separate target.

## 10.5 Longer or different outages

| Case | What happens |
|---|---|
| The outage is longer than the change log's retention (assumed ≥ 24 h) | Replay what's still there, then "records modified since" the start point gives current values (`via reconcile`, intermediate edits and actors lost). Beyond that, page "unrecoverable window T1–T2, full scan needed" (G4) |
| **Our Postgres** is down instead | The portal is down too, so no portal edits are lost. Webhooks get `503`. On recovery, replay from the last receiver heartbeat minus 10 minutes (G4) |
| Our worker restarts during the outage | Nothing changes; the rows wait in Postgres |
| Salesforce comes back but returns `429` | Pause all sending for `Retry-After`, keep the work (D11) |

## 10.6 What we watch during recovery

- The breaker's state, and the time it's been open (pages after 5 minutes, D24).
- **Proposed (Q10b, pending):** during the drain, M1 (oldest unsent change > 30 s) counts only **fresh-lane** rows,
  and a separate page fires if the backlog drains more than 25% slower than the formula predicts. Without this,
  M1 would page for the whole two hours of a normal drain.

# 9. The rule that stops a loop

Labels like `D17` point to [decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md). The steps are in [inbound.md](inbound.md) 5.2
and [outbound.md](outbound.md) 6.1.

## 9.1 The rule

**Only a portal user's save writes to the outbox. Nothing on the webhook path ever does.**

A change that came from Salesforce can never be sent back to Salesforce, so a loop is impossible by
construction, not by detection. Our own update coming back (an echo) is recognised so it doesn't create a
duplicate history row, but even if it weren't recognised it still couldn't be sent back.

| Writes to `sync.outbox` | Never writes to `sync.outbox` |
|---|---|
| `saveEdit()` in the portal backend, on a portal user's save (outbound.md 6.1) | The webhook receiver |
| The worker, only to change a row's status, key version or lease (never to add a row) | The worker applying a replay, a fetch or the sweep |
| | Any database trigger (there is none, by rule) |

## 9.2 How it's enforced

- **In code:** `saveEdit()` is the only function that inserts outbox rows. The apply function used by the
  receiver and the worker (`applyEvent`) has no outbox write in it.
- **In the database:** the `receiver` role has **no access** to `sync.outbox` at all (data.md 4.9).
- **By rule (CLAUDE.md):** no trigger writes the outbox, and no portal automation may call `saveEdit()` in
  reaction to a value a webhook applied. Either would turn a Salesforce change into an outgoing call.

## 9.3 Recognising our own echo

Every write we send carries `Portal_Change_Id__c = "ob_<outbox id>.<content_gen>"` (O1′). When Salesforce sends
the webhook for that write, the key is in `changedFields`. The receiver reads the outbox row from the key, and:

| Field in the echo | What happens (inbound.md 5.2) |
|---|---|
| **Kept exactly as we sent it** (row b) | The field keeps the portal save's time, actor and `editId`. `sfSeq` and `sfValue` move forward only if newer. **No history row**, because the portal save already wrote one |
| **Changed by Salesforce**, e.g. a phone reformatted (row c) | Applied as a Salesforce change, noted "normalised by Salesforce". **Not sent back**, by the rule in 9.1 |
| Any field, when a **newer** sales edit already reached us | Nothing moves backwards: `sfSeq` is already higher (I1) |

The echo also marks the outbox row `sent`. For an attempt whose reply was lost, that's the evidence that it
landed (outbound.md 6.6).

**Rejected ways to recognise an echo:**
- **"`changedBy` is the integration user"** on its own: it would also swallow genuine changes made by Salesforce
  automation running as that user.
- **"The value equals what we sent"**: it would swallow a real A → B → A change by a sales user.

## 9.4 Cases

| Case | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Finance's city write comes back as seq 4 | Echo, row b. The outbox row is `sent`; the field still shows finance; no history row; nothing is sent |
| Salesforce reformats our phone `9876543210` → `+91 98765 43210` | Row c. The portal shows the reformatted phone, noted "normalised by Salesforce". Nothing is sent |
| A Salesforce flow changes another field because of our write (a separate event, no key) | A normal Salesforce change, applied by the usual rules. Nothing is sent |
| The echo never arrives | The `2xx` reply already marked the row `sent`. A later replay that contains the event is dropped as a duplicate or treated as the echo |
| Our echo arrives after a newer sales edit to the same field | Row b changes nothing on that field; the sales value and its actor stay (I1) |
| Finance and sales keep overwriting each other's value | Each overwrite is a **human** save, each recorded in history. It's not a sync loop, and nothing repeats on its own (item 7) |

## 9.5 If a webhook carries the full record (the brief's "other case", D2)

With full-record webhooks, `Portal_Change_Id__c` is present on **every** event after our write, because it's a
field on the record, not just on our event.

- **Proposed rule (Q9, pending):** an event counts as our echo only if its key matches an outbox row **and**
  `changedBy` is the integration user. A later sales edit then carries the stale key but a sales `changedBy`,
  so it's applied as a normal Salesforce change.
- Unchanged fields repeated in a full-record webhook are no-ops: their `sequence` check or value comparison
  writes nothing new (inbound.md 5.2).
- The loop rule itself doesn't change: whatever the payload looks like, the webhook path never writes the
  outbox.

# 8. The rule for a duplicate webhook, and for an older webhook that arrives after a newer one

Labels like `D18` point to [decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md). The steps are in [inbound.md](inbound.md) 5.1
and 5.2; tables in [data.md](data.md).

We add one field to the brief's webhook: a per-record **`sequence`** (D4). Salesforce writes one record at a
time, so each change to a record gets the next number. The brief's `eventId` identifies a delivery; `sequence`
gives exact order and shows when one is missing.

## 8.1 Duplicate webhook

**Rule: a webhook whose `eventId` we have already stored is a duplicate. We reply `200` and change nothing.**

| Layer | Check | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| 1. `sync.inbox` | `INSERT (event_id, received_day, record_id, sequence) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Zero rows inserted means a duplicate. A second unique key, (`record_id`, `sequence`, `received_day`), catches the same change re-sent under a new `eventId` | Duplicates within the same day, including two copies arriving at the same moment (the second insert waits for the first to commit, then does nothing) |
| 2. Per-field `sfSeq` | A field is applied only if the event's `sequence` is **higher** than `field_meta[f].sfSeq` | Duplicates on a later day (the inbox is partitioned by day and the oldest day is dropped after 7 days), and anything else that slips past layer 1 |

- **Why `200`, not an error:** Salesforce did nothing wrong. A non-2xx reply would only make it retry.
- **Why the inbox is checked first, inside the same transaction as the apply:** a crash after the insert but
  before the commit rolls both back, so the retry is treated as new, not as a duplicate.
- **Replayed events go through the same inbox,** so the overlap between a replay and the webhooks we already
  have is dropped the same way (inbound.md 5.7).
- A duplicate caught only by layer 2 writes one extra history row marked `superseded` and never changes a
  value (T4).

**Example.** `evt_1001` (phone, seq 3) is delivered twice. The first is applied (inbound.md 5.5). The second's
inbox insert finds `(evt_1001, today)` and does nothing: `200`, no field, history or job is written.

## 8.2 Older webhook after a newer one

**Rule: for each field, apply an incoming value only if the event's `sequence` is higher than the `sequence`
that last set that field (`field_meta[f].sfSeq`). Judge each field separately. Always keep the event in history.**

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Seq 2 (phone A) arrives after seq 3 (phone B) | Phone stays B, because 2 ≤ 3. Phone A goes to history as `superseded` |
| Seq 2 changed **phone and email**, seq 3 changed only phone | Phone stays B. **Email from seq 2 lands**, because nothing newer has touched email |
| Seq 2 arrives and our portal value of that field is newer by time | Sequence check passes, time check keeps the portal value (item 7). `sfSeq` and `sfValue` still move to 2 |

- **Sequence first, time second.** The sequence check (inbound.md 5.2 row d) runs before the time comparison,

content.text:
I wrote all four sections in one go. Writing them turned up four questions, and **one is a real gap**: after a Salesforce outage, the replay would have started in the wrong place. Each question is marked "pending" where it appears in the files, and all four are logged as Phase 8 in [decisions.tmp.md](docs/decisions.tmp.md:457).

## The four files

| File | Outline item | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| [conflicts.md](docs/conflicts.md) | 7. Both sides change a record | **The rule:** each field on its own, the later `field_meta[f].updatedAt` wins. That's Salesforce's `occurredAt` against our Postgres clock taken inside the save transaction, and on a tie Salesforce wins. Where it's enforced on each of the four paths. The brief's cases, including two portal users (`409`). A worked example of a race while our write is in flight. What the losing user sees |
| [ordering.md](docs/ordering.md) | 8. Duplicate, and older after newer | **Duplicate:** the `eventId` is already in the inbox, so `200` and nothing changes, with the per-field `sfSeq` check as a second layer. **Older after newer:** a field is applied only if the event's `sequence` is higher than the field's `sfSeq`, and each field is judged separately. Gap detection and replay. The fallback if Salesforce sends no `sequence` |
| [loop.md](docs/loop.md) | 9. The rule that stops a loop | **The rule:** only a portal save writes to the outbox, so the webhook path never can. It's enforced in code, by database role and by CLAUDE.md. How we recognise our own echo from its key. Why we don't rely on `changedBy` or on equal values. Six cases, plus the full-record webhook case |
| [outage.md](docs/outage.md) | 10. The 6-hour outage | What happens during the outage. **On disk:** 432,000 outbox rows ≈ 216 MB. Recovery order, and why replaying first is now about avoiding a flood of `412`s rather than about correctness. **The arithmetic:** 60T = 438,338, so T ≈ **122 min**, or about 62 min if half the edits merge. Lanes, longer outages, what we watch |

---

❓ **Q10a - Where the replay starts after a Salesforce outage** (the real gap)

G4 said "replay from the last heartbeat minus 10 minutes". That works when **our Postgres** was down. But during a **Salesforce** outage our database is fine, so the heartbeat keeps beating, and that rule would start the replay at **recovery**. The whole 6-hour window would be missed.

Using the moment the breaker opened isn't safe either. In a quiet hour with no portal edits, we make no calls, so the breaker opens late, or never.

- **a. Start at the sweep's watermark minus 10 minutes.** The sweep runs every 5 minutes and stops advancing when its call fails, so its watermark is at most 5 minutes before the outage began, even in a quiet hour. For a database outage, use the earlier of this and the heartbeat.
  - Cost: up to 15 extra minutes of events. The replay is 30 × (21,600 + 900) = 675,000 events ÷ 2,000 = **338 calls**. The drain stays at about 122 min.
  - Pros: one point we already store, and nothing new to track.
  - Cons: the start point depends on the sweep job always running.
- **b. The time the breaker opened, minus 10 minutes.**
  - Cons: opens late in quiet periods, so events can be missed.
- **c. Track the time of the last successful Salesforce call of any kind, minus 10 minutes.**
  - Pros: precise.
  - Cons: a write on every call, and it's still stale in a quiet hour unless the sweep runs anyway.

➡️ **a.**

❓ **Q10b - M1 would page for the whole drain**

M1 pages when the oldest unsent change is more than 30 s old while Salesforce is reachable. During a normal 2-hour drain, the backlog's oldest row is hours old, so **M1 would page for two hours** about exactly what is supposed to happen.

- **a. During catch-up, M1 counts only fresh-lane rows. A separate page fires if the backlog drains more than 25% slower than the formula predicts.**
  - Pros: fresh edits are still held to 30 s, and a stuck drain still pages.
  - Cons: two rules instead of one.
- **b. Mute M1 until the backlog is empty.**
  - Cons: slow fresh edits go unnoticed for two hours.
- **c. Leave it as it is.**
  - Cons: two hours of paging, so people learn to ignore the alert.

➡️ **a.**

❓ **Q9 - Full-record webhooks (the brief's "other case")**

If Salesforce sent the whole record, `Portal_Change_Id__c` would appear on **every** event after our write, because it's a field on the record. A later sales edit would then look like our echo.

- **a. An event is our echo only if its key matches an outbox row *and* `changedBy` is the integration user.**
  - Pros: one extra condition, and sales edits are applied normally.
  - Cons: relies on Salesforce sending the integration user's email as `changedBy` for our writes. That's a reasonable assumption.
- **b. Compare the event's `sequence` with the version our reply returned.**
  - Cons: if the reply was lost, there's nothing to compare against.

➡️ **a.** This only matters in the full-record case. With changed-fields-only webhooks (our choice), the key appears only on our own event.

❓ **Q8 - A duplicate on a later day writes an extra history row**

The inbox drops its oldest day after 7 days. A duplicate that arrives on a later day passes the inbox check, then loses the sequence check, but still writes one history row marked superseded (T4). The value is always right, but the history has a duplicate line in it.

- **a. When every field of an event loses the sequence check, look in that record's history for the same `event_id` first. If it's there, write nothing.**
  - Pros: history stays clean. It only runs on this rare path, and one record's history is small.
  - Cons: one query across 13 monthly history partitions on that path.
- **b. Keep T4 as it is.**
  - Pros: nothing to add.
  - Cons: a duplicate line in an audit trail.

➡️ **a.**

Once you answer, I'll remove the "pending" markers. The Q10a fix also has to be carried into the G4 references in systems.md, data.md 4.7, outbound.md 6.10, subproblem 5, assumptions 1.3 and the numbers table, and CLAUDE.md rule 8. The 338-call figure replaces the older 324 and 333 wherever they appear.

# 10. The 6-hour outage: what is on disk, how we drain it, and the minutes of arithmetic

Labels like `D21` point to [decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md). Tables are in [data.md](data.md); the send
path is in [outbound.md](outbound.md).

The brief: the Salesforce API is unreachable for **6 hours**. Webhooks Salesforce tried to send in that window
may never arrive. Pending calls must survive our own restarts. The 30 s target applies only while both sides are
up; after the outage we **drain as fast as the rate limit allows**.

## 10.1 During the outage

| Part | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Detection** | After **5 failed calls in a row**, the circuit breaker opens. From then on, one test call every 30 s. Only a successful test closes it (D11) |
| **Portal** | Stays fully writable. A banner says "Salesforce sync paused: your changes are saved", and each changed record shows "pending sync" (D11) |
| **Outbox** | Every save still writes its row in the same transaction (outbound.md 6.1). Rows merge per record while `pending` |
| **Rows that were mid-send when it started** | Stay `sending` with the same key and content. Whether they landed is decided by evidence after recovery (outbound.md 6.6) |
| **Webhooks** | The receiver doesn't depend on the Salesforce API. Any webhook that does arrive is applied normally; the missing ones come back through the replay |
| **Sweep** | Fails like every other call, so its watermarks stop advancing. That frozen point is where the replay starts (10.3) |
| **Our restarts** | Nothing is lost: every pending call is a row in Postgres, and a `sending` row is picked up again when its lease has expired (outbound.md 6.3) |
| **Alert** | The breaker open for more than 5 minutes pages (D24) |

## 10.2 What is on disk after 6 hours

Worst case: the portal peak of **20 edits/s** lasts the full 6 h, and no two edits touch the same record, so
nothing merges.

| Where | Rows | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `sync.outbox` (pending, plus at most one `sending` row per record) | 20 × 21,600 = **432,000** | × ~500 B ≈ **216 MB** |
| `history`, one row per portal edit (already counted in the history budget, D15) | 432,000 | × ~200 B ≈ 86 MB |
| `sync.inbox`, only for webhooks that did arrive | up to 30 × 21,600 = 648,000 | × ~150 B ≈ 97 MB |
| `sync.watermarks` | the two sweep watermarks: the replay start | tiny |

Everything is in Postgres, written in the same transaction as the edit, so it survives any restart of our
processes. With merging, the outbox holds one row per edited record instead of one per edit.

## 10.3 Where the replay starts (Q10a)

**Replay start = the oldest completed sweep watermark, across customers and contacts, minus 10 minutes.** This
holds for any outage, Salesforce's or our database's: the sweep can't complete in either case, so its watermark
always sits before the outage began. (A heartbeat keeps beating during a Salesforce outage, so it can't mark
the start of one; G4's heartbeat rule is superseded.)

**When a watermark advances:**

| Event | `sweep:customers` / `sweep:contacts` |
|---|---|
| A sweep run starts at time S | Unchanged. The run reads "modified since watermark − 2 min", 2,000 records per page |
| Each page is applied | Unchanged |
| **The run's last page is applied and committed** | That object's watermark → **S** (the run's start, so changes made during the run are read again next time) |
| A page fails, or the worker stops mid-run | **Unchanged.** The next run starts again from the same point; re-applying is harmless (the apply rule only moves values forward) |
| **A change-log replay completes** | **Both** watermarks → the replay's start time, because the replay covered everything up to then |
| First deploy | Both set to the time the initial bulk load finished (D13) |

**Walk-through: a sweep that fails halfway.**

```
10:00:00  Sweep run: customers completes, contacts completes   -> customers 10:00:00, contacts 10:00:00
10:05:00  Sweep run starts (S = 10:05:00)
          customers: last page applied                          -> customers 10:05:00
          contacts: page 1 applied, page 2 call fails at 10:05:20 (the outage has begun)
                                                                -> contacts stays 10:00:00
10:10 ... 16:05  every sweep run fails                          -> both frozen
16:05:20  Breaker closes. Replay start = min(10:05:00, 10:00:00) - 10 min = 09:50:00
          Window 09:50:00 -> 16:05:20 = 22,520 s; 30 events/s x 22,520 = 675,600 events = 338 calls
16:09:50  Replay (started 16:05:20) completes                   -> customers 16:05:20, contacts 16:05:20
16:10:00  Normal sweeps resume from there
```

**Walk-through: a restart with one watermark missing.**

```
Before:   customers 10:05:00, contacts row missing (e.g. lost in a bad migration)
Restart:  the worker can't take a min() over a missing value, and must not treat it as "now"
          -> replay start = the change log's retention limit, now - 24 h
          -> page "sweep watermark missing: contacts"
          -> the next contacts sweep reads from the retention limit, then writes its watermark
Cost:     24 h x 30 events/s = 2,592,000 events = 1,296 calls; applying them ~17 min at 2,500 events/s.
          Rare, and safe: replayed events we already have are dropped by the normal rules.
```

## 10.4 Recovery order

1. **The breaker closes** on a successful test call.
2. **Replay Salesforce's change log** from the start point in 10.3. Each event goes through the inbox and the
   normal apply rule (`via replay`), so events we already have are dropped (item 8).
3. **Then drain the outbox** with a ramp of **20 → 40 → 80 req/s** (minute 1, minute 2, then on), in two lanes:
   **fresh** rows (created after recovery) and **backlog** rows, 50/50, each lane borrowing the other's unused
   share (D21).
4. Normal sweeps resume from the watermarks the replay set.

**Why replay first:** a queued 10:00 finance value must not overwrite an 11:00 sales edit from the outage. With
the replay applied first, the sales value's `editId` has replaced finance's, so the guard drops the stale field
before any call. The conditional update would also catch it (`412`), so replay-first isn't what makes this
correct any more; it avoids hundreds of thousands of `412`s at the start of the drain (V1).

## 10.5 The arithmetic

**Inputs**

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Outage | 6 h = 21,600 s | brief |
| Portal edits at peak | 20/s, for the whole outage and the recovery | assumption 1.1 |
| Salesforce edits at peak | 30/s | assumption 1.1 |
| Send rate | 80 req/s; 20 req/s of the 100 cap stays free for retries, `412` evidence, fetches and gap replays | assumption 3.1 |
| Ramp | 20 req/s in minute 1, 40 in minute 2, then 80 | D11 |
| Replay page | 2,000 events per call | assumption 1.3 |
| Sweep interval | 5 minutes, so the watermark is at most 5 minutes before the outage | G3 |
| Applying events | ~2,500 events/s (4 appliers split by record, ~1.6 ms per event each). To be measured | assumption 1.6 |

**Backlog:** 20 edits/s × 21,600 s = **432,000 calls**.

**Replay:** the six-hour window alone would be 30 × 21,600 = 648,000 events = 324 calls. The replay also covers
up to 15 minutes before it (up to 5 minutes of sweep staleness plus the 10-minute overlap): 30 events/s ×
(21,600 + 900) s = 675,000 events, and 675,000 ÷ 2,000 = **338 calls**.

**Drain, as fast as the rate limit allows.** Find T, in seconds after recovery, when everything sent equals
everything needed:

```
sent(T)   = 20 x 60  +  40 x 60  +  80 x (T - 120)  =  80T - 6,000      (ramp, then 80 req/s)
needed(T) = 432,000  +  338  +  20T                                      (backlog + replay calls + new portal edits)

80T - 6,000 = 432,338 + 20T
        60T = 438,338
          T = 438,338 / 60 = 7,305.6 s
          T = 7,305.6 / 60 = 121.8 min   ~ 122 minutes
```

**If half the outage edits hit a record already queued** (a guess; the real ratio is client question 9): the
backlog is 216,000 calls, so 60T = 216,000 + 338 + 6,000 = 222,338, and T = 222,338 ÷ 60 = 3,705.6 s ≈ **62
minutes**.

**What the 122 minutes includes, and what it doesn't.**

| Cost | Size | In the ~122 min? |
|---|---|---|
| The 338 replay **calls**, as a share of the rate limit | 338 calls | **Yes**: they're in `needed(T)` |
| The ramp's lost capacity | 6,000 calls | **Yes** |
| New portal edits during recovery | 20/s | **Yes** |
| **Fetching** the replay: pages follow a cursor, so they're sequential | 338 × ~200 ms ≈ **68 s** (at least 338 ÷ 20 = 17 s at minute 1's rate) | **No**: it overlaps with applying |
| **Applying** the 675,000 replayed events | 675,000 ÷ 2,500/s ≈ **270 s ≈ 4.5 min** | **No**: the formula assumes the drain isn't held up by it |

**End to end, with the replay applied strictly before the first outbox call:** the drain can only start after
R ≈ 270 s, and the 5,400 portal edits made meanwhile join it. With the replay calls already spent during R:

```
80t - 6,000 = 432,000 + 20 x (270 + t)
        60t = 443,400
          t = 7,390 s
total = 270 + 7,390 = 7,660 s = 127.7 min   ~ 128 minutes
```

So **122 minutes is the rate-limit answer the brief asks for**; **about 128 minutes is the planned end-to-end
time**, the difference being the time to apply the replay. Faster applying (more appliers) moves it towards 122.

**The order doesn't change the drain time.** The total to send and the rate are fixed, so the lanes decide only
*which* calls wait, not how long the drain takes.

## 10.6 When fresh edits are back under 30 s, and catching a stalled drain (Q10b)

**M1 during catch-up counts only fresh-lane rows** (created after recovery). Predicted fresh-lane backlog:

| Phase (time after recovery) | Fresh rows arriving | Fresh-lane send rate | Fresh rows waiting at the end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Replay, 0–270 s | 20/s | 0 (no outbox calls yet) | 5,400 |
| Ramp minute 1, 270–330 s | 20/s | 10/s (half of 20; the backlog lane is always busy, so there's nothing to borrow) | 6,000 |
| Ramp minute 2, 330–390 s | 20/s | 20/s (half of 40) | 6,000 |
| From 390 s | 20/s | 40/s (half of 80) | falls by 20/s: 6,000 ÷ 20 = 300 s |

The fresh lane is clear at about 390 + 300 = **690 s ≈ 11.5 minutes after recovery**. Edits made in the first
minutes of recovery can wait several minutes; that's the catch-up period the brief treats separately.

**Rule: M1 is re-armed when the fresh lane's oldest row first drops below 30 s after recovery, or 15 minutes after
recovery, whichever comes first. Once armed, it pages at > 30 s as usual.** The 15-minute cap stops a stuck
fresh lane from never being watched.

**Drain-stall rule.** Every minute, while the breaker is closed: if the backlog shrank by **less than 75% of
(allowed sends − fresh-lane sends) over the last 5 minutes**, page. "Shrank" counts backlog rows that left the
queue: sent, rejected, or emptied by the guard. A `429` pause counts as slowness, which is worth knowing.

**Example: the backlog stops shrinking 10 minutes into the drain.** By then the fresh lane is clear, so the
backlog runs at about 60/s, 3,600 rows a minute, and the 5-minute expectation is 18,000 rows; 75% of that is
13,500.

| Drain minute | Backlog rows cleared in the last 5 minutes | Page? |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 5 × 3,600 = 18,000 | no |

# 10. The 6-hour outage: what is on disk, how we drain it, and the minutes of arithmetic

Labels like `D21` point to [decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md). Tables are in [data.md](data.md); the send
path is in [outbound.md](outbound.md).

The brief: the Salesforce API is unreachable for **6 hours**. Webhooks Salesforce tried to send in that window
may never arrive. Pending calls must survive our own restarts. The 30 s target applies only while both sides are
up; after the outage we **drain as fast as the rate limit allows**.

## 10.1 During the outage

| Part | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Detection** | After **5 failed calls in a row**, the circuit breaker opens. From then on, one test call every 30 s. Only a successful test closes it (D11) |
| **Portal** | Stays fully writable. A banner says "Salesforce sync paused: your changes are saved", and each changed record shows "pending sync" (D11) |
| **Outbox** | Every save still writes its row in the same transaction (outbound.md 6.1). Rows merge per record while `pending` |
| **Rows that were mid-send when it started** | Stay `sending` with the same key and content. Whether they landed is decided by evidence after recovery (outbound.md 6.6) |
| **Webhooks** | The receiver doesn't depend on the Salesforce API. Any webhook that does arrive is applied normally; the missing ones come back through the replay |
| **Sweep** | Fails like every other call, so its watermarks stop advancing. That frozen point is where the replay starts (10.3) |
| **Our restarts** | Nothing is lost: every pending call is a row in Postgres, and a `sending` row is picked up again when its lease has expired (outbound.md 6.3) |
| **Alert** | The breaker open for more than 5 minutes pages (D24) |

## 10.2 What is on disk after 6 hours

Worst case: the portal peak of **20 edits/s** lasts the full 6 h, and no two edits touch the same record, so
nothing merges.

| Where | Rows | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `sync.outbox` (pending, plus at most one `sending` row per record) | 20 × 21,600 = **432,000** | × ~500 B ≈ **216 MB** |
| `history`, one row per portal edit (already counted in the history budget, D15) | 432,000 | × ~200 B ≈ 86 MB |
| `sync.inbox`, only for webhooks that did arrive | up to 30 × 21,600 = 648,000 | × ~150 B ≈ 97 MB |
| `sync.watermarks` | the two sweep watermarks: the replay start | tiny |

Everything is in Postgres, written in the same transaction as the edit, so it survives any restart of our
processes. With merging, the outbox holds one row per edited record instead of one per edit.

## 10.3 Where the replay starts (Q10a)

**Replay start = the oldest completed sweep watermark, across customers and contacts, minus 10 minutes.** This
holds for any outage, Salesforce's or our database's: the sweep can't complete in either case, so its watermark
always sits before the outage began. (A heartbeat keeps beating during a Salesforce outage, so it can't mark
the start of one; G4's heartbeat rule is superseded.)

**When a watermark advances:**

| Event | `sweep:customers` / `sweep:contacts` |
|---|---|
| A sweep run starts at time S | Unchanged. The run reads "modified since watermark − 2 min", 2,000 records per page |
| Each page is applied | Unchanged |
| **The run's last page is applied and committed** | That object's watermark → **S** (the run's start, so changes made during the run are read again next time) |
| A page fails, or the worker stops mid-run | **Unchanged.** The next run starts again from the same point; re-applying is harmless (the apply rule only moves values forward) |
| **A change-log replay completes** | **Both** watermarks → the replay's start time, because the replay covered everything up to then |
| First deploy | Both set to the time the initial bulk load finished (D13) |

**Walk-through: a sweep that fails halfway.**

```
10:00:00  Sweep run: customers completes, contacts completes   -> customers 10:00:00, contacts 10:00:00
10:05:00  Sweep run starts (S = 10:05:00)
          customers: last page applied                          -> customers 10:05:00
          contacts: page 1 applied, page 2 call fails at 10:05:20 (the outage has begun)
                                                                -> contacts stays 10:00:00
10:10 ... 16:05  every sweep run fails                          -> both frozen
16:05:20  Breaker closes. Replay start = min(10:05:00, 10:00:00) - 10 min = 09:50:00
          Window 09:50:00 -> 16:05:20 = 22,520 s; 30 events/s x 22,520 = 675,600 events = 338 calls
16:09:50  Replay (started 16:05:20) completes                   -> customers 16:05:20, contacts 16:05:20
16:10:00  Normal sweeps resume from there
```

**Walk-through: a restart with one watermark missing.**

```
Before:   customers 10:05:00, contacts row missing (e.g. lost in a bad migration)
Restart:  the worker can't take a min() over a missing value, and must not treat it as "now"
          -> replay start = the change log's retention limit, now - 24 h
          -> page "sweep watermark missing: contacts"
          -> the next contacts sweep reads from the retention limit, then writes its watermark
Cost:     24 h x 30 events/s = 2,592,000 events = 1,296 calls; applying them ~17 min at 2,500 events/s.
          Rare, and safe: replayed events we already have are dropped by the normal rules.
```

## 10.4 Recovery order

1. **The breaker closes** on a successful test call.
2. **Replay Salesforce's change log** from the start point in 10.3. Each event goes through the inbox and the
   normal apply rule (`via replay`), so events we already have are dropped (item 8).
3. **Then drain the outbox** with a ramp of **20 → 40 → 80 req/s** (minute 1, minute 2, then on), in two lanes:
   **fresh** rows (created after recovery) and **backlog** rows, 50/50, each lane borrowing the other's unused
   share (D21).
4. Normal sweeps resume from the watermarks the replay set.

**Why replay first:** a queued 10:00 finance value must not overwrite an 11:00 sales edit from the outage. With
the replay applied first, the sales value's `editId` has replaced finance's, so the guard drops the stale field
before any call. The conditional update would also catch it (`412`), so replay-first isn't what makes this
correct any more; it avoids hundreds of thousands of `412`s at the start of the drain (V1).

## 10.5 The arithmetic

**Inputs**

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Outage | 6 h = 21,600 s | brief |
| Portal edits at peak | 20/s, for the whole outage and the recovery | assumption 1.1 |
| Salesforce edits at peak | 30/s | assumption 1.1 |
| Send rate | 80 req/s; 20 req/s of the 100 cap stays free for retries, `412` evidence, fetches and gap replays | assumption 3.1 |
| Ramp | 20 req/s in minute 1, 40 in minute 2, then 80 | D11 |
| Replay page | 2,000 events per call | assumption 1.3 |
| Sweep interval | 5 minutes, so the watermark is at most 5 minutes before the outage | G3 |
| Applying events | ~2,500 events/s (4 appliers split by record, ~1.6 ms per event each). To be measured | assumption 1.6 |

**Backlog:** 20 edits/s × 21,600 s = **432,000 calls**.

**Replay:** the six-hour window alone would be 30 × 21,600 = 648,000 events = 324 calls. The replay also covers
up to 15 minutes before it (up to 5 minutes of sweep staleness plus the 10-minute overlap): 30 events/s ×
(21,600 + 900) s = 675,000 events, and 675,000 ÷ 2,000 = **338 calls**.

**Drain, as fast as the rate limit allows.** Find T, in seconds after recovery, when everything sent equals
everything needed:

```
sent(T)   = 20 x 60  +  40 x 60  +  80 x (T - 120)  =  80T - 6,000      (ramp, then 80 req/s)
needed(T) = 432,000  +  338  +  20T                                      (backlog + replay calls + new portal edits)

80T - 6,000 = 432,338 + 20T
        60T = 438,338
          T = 438,338 / 60 = 7,305.6 s
          T = 7,305.6 / 60 = 121.8 min   ~ 122 minutes
```

**If half the outage edits hit a record already queued** (a guess; the real ratio is client question 9): the
backlog is 216,000 calls, so 60T = 216,000 + 338 + 6,000 = 222,338, and T = 222,338 ÷ 60 = 3,705.6 s ≈ **62
minutes**.

**What the 122 minutes includes, and what it doesn't.**

| Cost | Size | In the ~122 min? |
|---|---|---|
| The 338 replay **calls**, as a share of the rate limit | 338 calls | **Yes**: they're in `needed(T)` |
| The ramp's lost capacity | 6,000 calls | **Yes** |
| New portal edits during recovery | 20/s | **Yes** |
| **Fetching** the replay: pages follow a cursor, so they're sequential | 338 × ~200 ms ≈ **68 s** (at least 338 ÷ 20 = 17 s at minute 1's rate) | **No**: it overlaps with applying |
| **Applying** the 675,000 replayed events | 675,000 ÷ 2,500/s ≈ **270 s ≈ 4.5 min** | **No**: the formula assumes the drain isn't held up by it |

**End to end, with the replay applied strictly before the first outbox call:** the drain can only start after
R ≈ 270 s, and the 5,400 portal edits made meanwhile join it. With the replay calls already spent during R:

```
80t - 6,000 = 432,000 + 20 x (270 + t)
        60t = 443,400
          t = 7,390 s
total = 270 + 7,390 = 7,660 s = 127.7 min   ~ 128 minutes
```

So **122 minutes is the rate-limit answer the brief asks for**; **about 128 minutes is the planned end-to-end
time**, the difference being the time to apply the replay. Faster applying (more appliers) moves it towards 122.

**The order doesn't change the drain time.** The total to send and the rate are fixed, so the lanes decide only
*which* calls wait, not how long the drain takes.

## 10.6 When fresh edits are back under 30 s, and catching a stalled drain (Q10b)

**M1 during catch-up counts only fresh-lane rows** (created after recovery). Predicted fresh-lane backlog:

| Phase (time after recovery) | Fresh rows arriving | Fresh-lane send rate | Fresh rows waiting at the end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Replay, 0–270 s | 20/s | 0 (no outbox calls yet) | 5,400 |
| Ramp minute 1, 270–330 s | 20/s | 10/s (half of 20; the backlog lane is always busy, so there's nothing to borrow) | 6,000 |
| Ramp minute 2, 330–390 s | 20/s | 20/s (half of 40) | 6,000 |
| From 390 s | 20/s | 40/s (half of 80) | falls by 20/s: 6,000 ÷ 20 = 300 s |

The fresh lane is clear at about 390 + 300 = **690 s ≈ 11.5 minutes after recovery**. Edits made in the first
minutes of recovery can wait several minutes; that's the catch-up period the brief treats separately.

**Rule: M1 is re-armed when the fresh lane's oldest row first drops below 30 s after recovery, or 15 minutes after

**Example: the backlog stops shrinking 10 minutes into the drain.** By then the fresh lane is clear, so the

13,500.

|---|---|---|
| 10 | 5 × 3,600 = 18,000 | no |
| 11 | 4 × 3,600 + 0 = 14,400 | no (≥ 13,500) |
| **12** | 3 × 3,600 = 10,800 | **yes** (< 13,500) |

| Case | What happens |
|---|---|
| The outage is longer than the change log's retention (assumed ≥ 24 h) | Replay what's still there, then "records modified since" the start point gives current values (`via reconcile`, intermediate edits and actors lost). Beyond that, page "unrecoverable window T1–T2, full scan needed" (G4) |

| Salesforce comes back but returns `429` | Pause all sending for `Retry-After`, keep the work (D11). The drain-stall rule pages if it lasts |

# 10. The 6-hour outage: what is on disk, how we drain it, and the minutes of arithmetic

Labels like `D21` point to [decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md). Tables are in [data.md](data.md); the send
path is in [outbound.md](outbound.md).

The brief: the Salesforce API is unreachable for **6 hours**. Webhooks Salesforce tried to send in that window
may never arrive. Pending calls must survive our own restarts. The 30 s target applies only while both sides are
up; after the outage we **drain as fast as the rate limit allows**.

## 10.1 During the outage

| Part | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Detection** | After **5 failed calls in a row**, the circuit breaker opens. From then on, one test call every 30 s. Only a successful test closes it (D11) |
| **Portal** | Stays fully writable. A banner says "Salesforce sync paused: your changes are saved", and each changed record shows "pending sync" (D11) |
| **Outbox** | Every save still writes its row in the same transaction (outbound.md 6.1). Rows merge per record while `pending` |
| **Rows that were mid-send when it started** | Stay `sending` with the same key and content. Whether they landed is decided by evidence after recovery (outbound.md 6.6) |
| **Webhooks** | The receiver doesn't depend on the Salesforce API. Any webhook that does arrive is applied normally; the missing ones come back through the replay |
| **Sweep** | Fails like every other call, so its watermark stops advancing. That frozen watermark is where the replay starts (10.3) |
| **Our restarts** | Nothing is lost: every pending call is a row in Postgres, and a `sending` row is picked up again when its lease has expired (outbound.md 6.3) |
| **Alert** | The breaker open for more than 5 minutes pages (D24) |

## 10.2 What is on disk after 6 hours

Worst case: the portal peak of **20 edits/s** lasts the full 6 h, and no two edits touch the same record, so
nothing merges.

| Where | Rows | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `sync.outbox` (pending, plus at most one `sending` row per record) | 20 × 21,600 = **432,000** | × ~500 B ≈ **216 MB** |
| `history`, one row per portal edit (already counted in the history budget, D15) | 432,000 | × ~200 B ≈ 86 MB |
| `sync.inbox`, only for webhooks that did arrive | up to 30 × 21,600 = 648,000 | × ~150 B ≈ 97 MB |
| `sync.watermarks` | the sweep's last successful point (the replay start) | tiny |

Everything is in Postgres, written in the same transaction as the edit, so it survives any restart of our
processes. With merging, the outbox holds one row per edited record instead of one per edit.

## 10.3 Recovery order

1. **The breaker closes** on a successful test call.
2. **Replay Salesforce's change log first** (D3, D21), for the whole window in which webhooks may have been lost.
   **Proposed start point (Q10a, pending):** the sweep's watermark minus 10 minutes. The sweep runs every 5
   minutes, so its watermark is at most 5 minutes before the outage began, even in a quiet hour when nothing
   else would have noticed the outage. Each replayed event goes through the inbox and the normal apply rule
   (`via replay`), so events we already have are dropped.
3. **Drain the outbox** with a ramp of **20 → 40 → 80 req/s** (minute 1, minute 2, then on), in two lanes:
   **fresh** rows (created after recovery) and **backlog** rows, 50/50, each lane borrowing the other's unused
   share (D21).
4. The sweep resumes and catches anything the replay couldn't return.

**Why replay first:** a queued 10:00 finance value must not overwrite an 11:00 sales edit from the outage. With
the replay applied first, the sales value's `editId` has replaced finance's, so the guard drops the stale field
before any call. The conditional update would also catch it (`412`), so replay-first is no longer what makes
this correct; it's what avoids hundreds of thousands of `412`s at the start of the drain (V1).

## 10.4 The arithmetic

**Inputs**

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Outage | 6 h = 21,600 s | brief |
| Portal edits at peak | 20/s, for the whole outage and the drain | assumption 1.1 |
| Salesforce edits at peak | 30/s | assumption 1.1 |
| Send rate | 80 req/s; 20 req/s of the 100 cap stays free for retries, `412` evidence, fetches and gap replays | assumption 3.1 |
| Ramp | 20 req/s in minute 1, 40 in minute 2, then 80 | D11 |
| Replay page | 2,000 events per call | assumption 1.3 |

**Backlog:** 20 edits/s × 21,600 s = **432,000 calls**.

**Replay:** the window is the outage plus up to 15 minutes before it (up to 5 minutes of sweep staleness plus the
10-minute overlap): 30 events/s × (21,600 + 900) s = 675,000 events, and 675,000 ÷ 2,000 = **338 calls**.

**Drain.** Find the time T, in seconds after recovery, when everything sent equals everything needed:

```
sent(T)   = 20 x 60  +  40 x 60  +  80 x (T - 120)  =  80T - 6,000      (ramp, then 80 req/s)
needed(T) = 432,000  +  338  +  20T                                      (backlog + replay + new portal edits)

80T - 6,000 = 432,338 + 20T
        60T = 438,338
          T = 438,338 / 60 = 7,305.6 s
          T = 7,305.6 / 60 = 121.8 min   ~ 122 minutes
```

**If half the outage edits hit a record already queued** (a guess; the real ratio is client question 9): the
backlog is 216,000 calls, so 60T = 216,000 + 338 + 6,000 = 222,338, and T = 222,338 ÷ 60 = 3,705.6 s ≈ **62
minutes**.

**The order doesn't change the time.** The total to send and the rate are fixed, so the lanes decide only *which*
calls wait, not how long the drain takes. Per lane after the ramp: fresh edits arrive at 20/s against a 40/s lane,
so they go out within about a second; the backlog gets the remaining 60/s and still finishes at about 122
minutes. During the 2-minute ramp, fresh edits can wait longer than 30 s; that's inside the catch-up period, which
the brief treats as a separate target.

## 10.5 Longer or different outages

| Case | What happens |
|---|---|
| The outage is longer than the change log's retention (assumed ≥ 24 h) | Replay what's still there, then "records modified since" the start point gives current values (`via reconcile`, intermediate edits and actors lost). Beyond that, page "unrecoverable window T1–T2, full scan needed" (G4) |
| **Our Postgres** is down instead | The portal is down too, so no portal edits are lost. Webhooks get `503`. On recovery, replay from the last receiver heartbeat minus 10 minutes (G4) |
| Our worker restarts during the outage | Nothing changes; the rows wait in Postgres |
| Salesforce comes back but returns `429` | Pause all sending for `Retry-After`, keep the work (D11) |

## 10.6 What we watch during recovery

- The breaker's state, and the time it's been open (pages after 5 minutes, D24).
- **Proposed (Q10b, pending):** during the drain, M1 (oldest unsent change > 30 s) counts only **fresh-lane** rows,
  and a separate page fires if the backlog drains more than 25% slower than the formula predicts. Without this,
  M1 would page for the whole two hours of a normal drain.

Beyond that: a page, "unrecoverable window T1–T2, full scan needed" | One primary is enough at 50 edits/s. A replica for failover is out of scope this weekend |
| `sync.heartbeat` | receiver | worker | Last time the receiver could write. After a database outage, replay starts here minus 10 minutes (G4) |
## 5. Outage catch-up

- **What:** after the breaker closes, or after our own database comes back:
  1. **Replay Salesforce's change log first:** from the last receiver heartbeat before the outage minus a 10-minute overlap (G4), falling back to "modified since T". Not from "the last `eventId` we applied", because webhooks arrive out of order. The overlap's duplicates are dropped by the inbox and `sequence`.
  2. **Then drain** with a ramp of 20 → 40 → 80 req/s, split **50/50 between fresh edits and the backlog, each borrowing the other's unused share**. The lane comes from `created_at` against the recovery time.
- **Why fifth:** it builds on 3 and 4. Replaying first is what stops an older queued portal value overwriting a newer sales edit made during the outage.
- **Decisions:** D3, D11, D21, G4.
- **Arithmetic it must reproduce (scaled down in a demo):**
  - **Backlog:** 432,000 calls.
  - **Replay:** 324 calls, plus 9 for the 10-minute overlap (30 edits/s × 600 s ÷ 2,000). The drain stays at about 122 min (60T = 438,333).
  - **Drain:** 60T = 438,324, so about **122 min** in the worst case, or about 62 min if 50% merged.
- **Done when:** after a simulated outage, replay finishes before the first outbound call. Fresh edits sync in under 30 s once the ramp ends. The backlog drains in the time the formula predicts for the configured cap.

## 6. Webhook endpoint wrapper

| Database outage recovery | After Postgres returns, replay from the last heartbeat minus 10 minutes. Beyond the log's retention, "modified since". Beyond that, page "unrecoverable window" | G4 |
### 1.3 Changes made during the 6-hour outage (D3)
- **Question:** Can we ask Salesforce for the records that changed during the 6 hours, or are those changes gone unless we already have them?
- **Assumption:**
  - Salesforce keeps a **replayable change log**: "give me every event from time T". We replay from the last receiver heartbeat before the outage minus a 10-minute overlap, not from "the last `eventId` we applied", because webhooks arrive out of order (G4).
  - The log is kept for **at least 24 h**.
  - Each request returns a page of **2,000 events**.
  - **Fallback (worst case):** if the log has expired, query records modified since the outage began.
- **If the answer goes the other way:**
  - **With the fallback query only:** we get current values only, so edits in between and their actors are lost. History records them as "reconciled after outage, intermediate edits unknown".
  - **With neither:** we need a full scan of 5M records, at least 2,500 calls.

## 5. Numbers used in the arithmetic

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Portal edits at peak | 20/s | assumption 1.1 |
| Salesforce edits at peak | 30/s | assumption 1.1 |
| Quiet-hour edits | 1/s each side | assumption 1.1 |
| Salesforce API cap | 100 req/s | brief |
| Our normal send rate | 80 req/s (20 req/s headroom) | assumption 3.1 |
| Rate during the outage | ~0 (one test call every 30 s) | D11 |
| Ramp after recovery | 20 req/s (minute 1) → 40 (minute 2) → 80 | D11 |
| Outage length | 6 h = 21,600 s | brief |
| Portal backlog after the outage | 20 × 21,600 = **432,000 calls** | derived |
| Salesforce events to replay | 30 × 21,600 = 648,000 → ÷ 2,000 per page = **324 calls** | assumption 1.3 |
| Drain time, worst case | 60T = 438,324 → T ≈ 7,305 s ≈ **122 min** | D21 |
| Drain time, 50% merged (guess) | 60T = 222,000 → T ≈ 3,700 s ≈ **62 min** | D21 |
| Outbox on disk after the outage | ~432,000 × 500 B ≈ **216 MB** (less with merging) | D21 |
| Sync target while both sides are up | 30 s worst case | brief |

How the drain time is computed:

```
sent(T)   = 1,200 + 2,400 + 80 x (T - 120) = 80T - 6,000   (ramp, then 80 req/s)
needed(T) = 432,000 + 20T                                    (backlog + new edits)
80T - 6,000 = 432,000 + 20T  ->  60T = 438,000  ->  T = 7,300 s ~ 122 min
```

Replaying first takes 324 of minute 1's 1,200 calls, so the sum becomes 60T = 438,324, T ≈ 7,305 s, still about 122 min.

---
216:### 4.4 How often outage edits hit the same record (D21)
217-- **Question:** During 6 hours, how many portal edits land on a record already waiting to be sent?
218-- **Assumption:** unknown. We present the **worst case with no merging (122 min)** as the headline. A **50% guess (about 62 min)** shows what merging is worth.
219-- **If the answer goes the other way:** with real logs we'd replace the guess with the actual ratio. The worst case stays the same.
220-
221----
222-

content.text:
All four decisions are closed with the cases you asked for. Every "pending" marker is gone, and the cross-references are updated.

## Q10a: the sweep watermark ([outage.md](docs/outage.md) 10.3, 10.5)

- **The rule:** the replay starts at the **oldest** completed watermark (customers, contacts) minus 10 minutes. This works for any outage, Salesforce's or our database's, because the sweep can't complete in either case. G4's heartbeat is superseded as the replay start and stays only as a diagnostic.
- **When a watermark moves:** a table covers every case:
  - It moves forward only when a run's last page is applied, and then to that run's **start** time.
  - A completed replay moves both watermarks to the replay's start time.
  - A failed or interrupted run leaves it unchanged.
  - On first deploy, both are set to the end of the bulk load.
- **A sweep that fails halfway:** customers reaches 10:05, while contacts stays at 10:00 because its second page failed at 10:05:20. The replay starts at min(10:05, 10:00) − 10 min = **09:50**. That's 675,600 events, or 338 calls. When the replay finishes, both watermarks move to 16:05:20.
- **A restart with one watermark missing:** never treated as "now". The replay starts from the change log's retention limit (24 h back), and a page fires. That costs 1,296 calls and about 17 minutes of applying. Rare, and safe.
- **What 122 minutes includes:**

  | Cost | In the 122 min? |
  |---|---|
  | The 338 replay calls, as a share of the rate limit | Yes |
  | The ramp, and new portal edits during recovery | Yes |
  | Fetching the replay, about 68 s because pages follow a cursor | No: it overlaps with applying |
  | Applying the 675,000 events, about **270 s** at an assumed 2,500 events/s (new assumption 4.5) | No |

  **End to end, with the replay applied first:** 60t = 443,400, so t = 7,390 s, and the total is 7,660 s ≈ **128 min**. So 122 minutes is the rate-limit answer the brief asks for, and 128 minutes is the planned time from recovery to an empty outbox.

## Q10b: fresh-lane M1 and catching a stalled drain (outage.md 10.6)

- **Predicted fresh-lane backlog:** fresh edits pile up during the replay and the ramp (6,000 rows), then clear at 20/s. The lane is clear at about **11.5 minutes after recovery**.
- **When the 30 s alert applies again:** when the fresh lane's oldest row first drops below 30 s, or 15 minutes after recovery, whichever is first.
- **The drain-stall page:** every minute, page if the backlog shrank by less than 75% of (allowed sends − fresh-lane sends) over the last 5 minutes. **If the backlog stops shrinking at minute 10 of the drain, the page fires at minute 12:**
  - at minute 11, the last 5 minutes cleared 14,400 rows, at or above the 13,500 threshold
  - at minute 12, they cleared 10,800, below it

  That's about 110 minutes before the predicted finish.

## Q9: the automation case ([loop.md](docs/loop.md) 9.5)

You were right: an automation running as the integration user passes both proposed checks, and **nothing in a full snapshot proves our key belongs to that event.** So in full-snapshot mode:
- The echo rules are never applied from a snapshot.
- A field equal to our current value changes nothing, so finance's city doesn't flip to the integration user.
- A different value is a normal Salesforce change, with its actor set to `changedBy`.
- **A snapshot never confirms an uncertain send.** That can only be the reply, a change-log event that lists our key among **its own** changed fields, or the last-resort GET.

**One note I added there:** the GET is the same kind of evidence as a snapshot. Seeing our key on the record proves an attempt with that key landed *at some point*, but not which event delivered it. So the GET is documented as the last fallback only.

## Q8: the history check ([ordering.md](docs/ordering.md) 8.1)

A side-by-side table shows the two cases:
- **The same event replayed the next day:** it passes the inbox and loses the sequence check. History already has a row with the same `event_id` and `sf_seq`, so **0 history rows** are written.
- **A genuinely older event (seq 2):** it also passes the inbox and loses the sequence check. History has nothing with its ID or sequence, so **1 superseded row** is written.

The check matches on `event_id` **or** `sf_seq`. So a replay that sends the same record and sequence under a **different** `event_id` is still caught: on the same day by the inbox's second key, and on a later day by `sf_seq`.

❓ **R1 - Number 1 would page forever on contacts waiting behind a rejected customer**

When a customer's create is rejected, its contacts' rows are parked until someone fixes the customer (O3′). They stay unconfirmed for hours, so number 1 would page all night about something only a user can fix.

- **b. Count them anyway.**
  - Cons: a false page that won't clear until a user acts.
- **c. A separate fourth number for parked rows.**
  - Cons: the brief asks for three.

➡️ **a.**

❓ **R2 - Number 2 goes silent if webhooks stop arriving**

  - Cons: it fires up to about 10 minutes late, not 30 s.
- **b. Page if no webhook arrives for 15 minutes during working hours.**
  - Pros: simple.
  - Cons: false alarms on a quiet afternoon, and it misses partial loss (some webhooks arriving, others not).
- **c. Keep only the delay and the gap rule.**
  - Cons: misses a total stop. A gap is only noticed when a *later* webhook arrives.

➡️ **a.**

❓ **R3 - What number 3 counts**

Some replies would inflate or duplicate it:
- **`412`s** are normal when both sides edit the same record (G1). That isn't Salesforce failing.
- **`429`s** mean Salesforce is throttling us.
- **While the breaker is open**, every test call fails, so the rate is 100%, which duplicates the breaker alert.

- **a. Count `5xx`, timeouts, and `4xx` except `412`, over all calls including retries. Track `412` and `429` beside it, without counting them in the rate. Don't evaluate it while the breaker is open.**
  - Pros: the number means "Salesforce is failing us". Busy conflict periods don't page. One outage gives one page (the breaker's), not two. A long run of `429`s still pages through the drain-stall rule (Q10b).
  - Cons: a storm of `412`s isn't paged by this number. It's still visible, and G1b's back-off after 5 `412`s in a row records it.
- **b. Count every non-`2xx`.**
  - Cons: conflicts and throttling look like outages, and an outage pages twice.
- **c. Count only `5xx` and timeouts.**
  - Cons: misses a new Salesforce validation rule silently rejecting our updates. That's what the `4xx` > 1% condition exists to catch.

➡️ **a.**

# 11. Three numbers we watch, and when we call someone

Labels like `D24` and `R1` point to [decisions.tmp.md](decisions.tmp.md). Tables are in [data.md](data.md).
Metrics and alerts are **described, not built** this weekend (D26).

The three numbers cover the three ways the sync fails a user: a portal change doesn't reach Salesforce, a
Salesforce change doesn't reach the portal, or Salesforce starts refusing us. The red line follows the brief's
30-second worst case (D24).

## 11.1 Summary

| # | Number | Page when |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Oldest unconfirmed portal edit** | > **30 s**, while the breaker is closed. Plus: the breaker open > **5 min**; during recovery, the fresh-lane re-arm rule and the drain-stall page |
| **2** | **Salesforce-to-portal delay** | p95 > **30 s** over 5 min; a sequence gap unfilled after **10 min**; or **two successful sweeps in a row** each find a change the webhooks missed |
| **3** | **Salesforce API failure rate** | > **5%** of attempts fail over 5 min, or > **1%** are validation or permission rejections |

## 11.2 Number 1: oldest unconfirmed portal edit

**Definition:** `now − age_from` of the oldest outbox row whose status is `pending` or `sending`.

| Detail | Rule |
|---|---|
| **What counts** | `pending` rows and `sending` rows, including a row whose send is **uncertain** and still waiting for evidence that it landed (outbound.md 6.6). "Unconfirmed" catches a send stuck in that state; "unsent" would miss it |
| **`age_from`** | The row's `created_at`, except as below (R1) |
| **Excluded: a contact blocked by a rejected customer create** (R1) | While a contact's row is parked because its customer's create was **rejected** by Salesforce, it's left out (`blocked_by = 'rejected_customer'`). The rejection stays visible in the portal ("waiting for customer: rejected by Salesforce") and is already counted by number 3 |
| **When the block ends** | When the customer gets its `sf_id`, the row becomes eligible to send again: `link_contacts` clears `blocked_by` and sets **`age_from = now()`**, so its 30-second timer starts then, not from the original save |
| **A contact waiting for a customer that's merely in flight** | Not excluded. It should be sent within 30 s like any other edit |
| **Page** | Oldest > 30 s while the breaker is closed |

**Example (R1).**

```
09:00  Finance creates customer Acme (no name) and contact Ravi -> Ravi's row parked behind Acme
09:00  Acme's create is rejected: Name required
       -> Ravi's row: blocked_by = 'rejected_customer'; excluded from number 1
       -> portal shows "waiting for customer: rejected by Salesforce"; number 3 counts the 4xx
14:00  Finance adds the name; Acme's new upsert is sent (Acme's own row is counted normally)
14:00:01  Acme gets its sf_id -> link_contacts wakes Ravi's row: blocked_by = NULL, age_from = 14:00:01
14:00:02  Ravi is sent -> age 1 s, well under 30 s. Five hours parked never paged
```

**During an outage and recovery** (outage.md 10.6):
- **Breaker open:** the 30-second rule doesn't apply (the brief's target is "while both sides are up"). The breaker
  open for more than **5 minutes** pages instead.
- **Catch-up:** only **fresh-lane** rows (created after recovery) count. The 30-second rule re-arms when the
  fresh lane's oldest row first drops below 30 s, or 15 minutes after recovery, whichever is first (about 11.5
  minutes, predicted).
- **Drain stall:** every minute, page if the backlog shrank by less than 75% of (allowed sends − fresh-lane
  sends) over the last 5 minutes. A backlog that stops shrinking 10 minutes into the drain pages at minute 12.
- **Sustained throttling** (`429`s): in normal operation, rows age past 30 s and number 1 pages; during
  recovery, the drain-stall rule pages.

## 11.3 Number 2: Salesforce-to-portal delay

**Definition:** for each webhook applied, **our commit time − `occurredAt`**.

| Condition | Page when | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Delay** | p95 > 30 s over 5 minutes | The brief's 30-second target for Salesforce → portal |
| **Gap** | A sequence gap still unfilled after 10 minutes | A specific webhook is lost and the per-record replay (D19) couldn't fill it |
| **Sweep fallback** (R2) | **Two consecutive successful sweeps each find at least one Salesforce change the webhook path missed** | Webhooks stopping altogether gives number 2 no samples, so it can't page on delay. The sweep compares Salesforce with us every 5 minutes |

- **What the sweep counts as missed:** a record whose Salesforce values are newer than ours and different, last
  changed **more than 60 s before the sweep read it**. A change younger than that is left for the next run, so a
  webhook still in flight isn't counted as a miss.
- **One miss doesn't page.** The sweep repairs it and records it in history (`via reconcile`). Two runs in a row
  with misses means webhooks are being lost repeatedly, and that pages.
- **A failed sweep run** neither counts nor breaks the streak; only successful runs are compared.
- **It's a fallback**, with a detection window of about **10 minutes** (two 5-minute runs), not 30 s. It catches
  a broken webhook subscription and steady partial loss that the delay and gap rules can't see.
- **Replayed events don't count in the delay.** After an outage, replayed events have hours of delay by design;
  only webhooks are measured.

## 11.4 Number 3: Salesforce API failure rate

**Definition:** over 5 minutes, failed attempts ÷ all attempts to the Salesforce API, **retries included** in the
total.

| Reply | In the failure rate? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Timeout | **Yes** | |
| `5xx` | **Yes** | |
| `4xx` other than `412` and `429` | **Yes** | Includes validation (`400`) and permission (`401` after one token refresh, `403`) |
| `412` | No, tracked separately | Normal when both sides edit the same record (G1). Back-off after 5 in a row is recorded (G1b) |
| `429` | No, tracked separately | Throttling, not failure. Sustained throttling is caught by number 1 or the drain-stall rule |
| `2xx` | No (it's in the total) | |

| Page when | Catches |
|---|---|
| **> 5%** of attempts fail | Salesforce degrading, network trouble, our credentials breaking |
| **> 1%** of attempts are **validation or permission rejections** | A new validation rule, a field-level permission change, or a rejected create (the R1 case). Users' edits are being refused |

- **Not evaluated while the breaker is open.** Every test call fails then; the breaker's own 5-minute page covers
  the outage, so one outage gives one page.
- **Outage probes are excluded** from the rate after the breaker closes, so the test calls made during the outage
  don't keep the rate high once Salesforce is back.

## 11.5 Pages that sit beside the three numbers

These aren't separate numbers; they're conditions on the same data, already decided elsewhere.

| Page | From |
|---|---|
| Breaker open > 5 min | Number 1 during an outage (D24) |
| Drain stall | Number 1 during recovery (Q10b) |
| Sweep watermark missing | outage.md 10.3 (Q10a) |
| `Portal_Id__c` row holding a different `sf_id` | inbound.md 5.3 (I2); counted in number 3 |
| Unrecoverable replay window, full scan needed | outage.md 10.7 (G4) |

## 11.6 What the three numbers don't catch

| Blind spot | Where it shows instead |
|---|---|
| A forgotten customer whose create was rejected | The portal badge, and number 3's rejection rate when it happened |
| A storm of `412`s on a hot record | The separate `412` count and the G1b back-off |
| Clock skew between Salesforce and us beyond the assumed 1 s | Number 2 drifting high or negative; no page of its own |
| A single lost webhook on a record never edited again | Repaired by the next sweep; pages only if misses repeat (R2) |

Salesforce change doesn't reach the portal, or Salesforce starts refusing us. The red line follows the brief's
30-second worst case (D24).

| # | Number | Page when |

| **2** | **Salesforce-to-portal delay** | p95 > **30 s** over 5 min; a sequence gap unfilled after **10 min**; or **two successful sweeps in a row** each find a change the webhooks missed |
| **3** | **Salesforce API failure rate** | > **5%** of attempts fail over 5 min, or > **1%** are validation or permission rejections |

## 11.2 Number 1: oldest unconfirmed portal edit

**Definition:** `now − age_from` of the oldest outbox row whose status is `pending` or `sending`.

| Detail | Rule |
|---|---|
| **What counts** | `pending` rows and `sending` rows, including a row whose send is **uncertain** and still waiting for evidence that it landed (outbound.md 6.6). "Unconfirmed" catches a send stuck in that state; "unsent" would miss it |
| **`age_from`** | The row's `created_at`, except as below (R1) |
| **Excluded: a contact blocked by a rejected customer create** (R1) | While a contact's row is parked because its customer's create was **rejected** by Salesforce, it's left out (`blocked_by = 'rejected_customer'`). The rejection stays visible in the portal ("waiting for customer: rejected by Salesforce") and is already counted by number 3 |
| **When the block ends** | When the customer gets its `sf_id`, the row becomes eligible to send again: `link_contacts` clears `blocked_by` and sets **`age_from = now()`**, so its 30-second timer starts then, not from the original save |
| **A contact waiting for a customer that's merely in flight** | Not excluded. It should be sent within 30 s like any other edit |
| **Page** | Oldest > 30 s while the breaker is closed |

**Example (R1).**

```
09:00  Finance creates customer Acme (no name) and contact Ravi -> Ravi's row parked behind Acme
09:00  Acme's create is rejected: Name required

14:00  Finance adds the name; Acme's new upsert is sent (Acme's own row is counted normally)
14:00:01  Acme gets its sf_id -> link_contacts wakes Ravi's row: blocked_by = NULL, age_from = 14:00:01
14:00:02  Ravi is sent -> age 1 s, well under 30 s. Five hours parked never paged
```

**During an outage and recovery** (outage.md 10.6):

  open for more than **5 minutes** pages instead.
- **Catch-up:** only **fresh-lane** rows (created after recovery) count. The 30-second rule re-arms when the
  fresh lane's oldest row first drops below 30 s, or 15 minutes after recovery, whichever is first (about 11.5
  minutes, predicted).
- **Drain stall:** every minute, page if the backlog shrank by less than 75% of (allowed sends − fresh-lane
  sends) over the last 5 minutes. A backlog that stops shrinking 10 minutes into the drain pages at minute 12.

  - Behaviour during an outage and catch-up: the breaker page after 5 minutes, the fresh-lane re-arm, the drain-stall page, and how sustained throttling shows up.
- **11.3 Number 2, Salesforce-to-portal delay:** the p95 delay and gap rules stay.
  - **R2:** page when two consecutive **successful** sweeps each find at least one change the webhooks missed. It's described as a fallback with a roughly 10-minute detection window. One miss is repaired and recorded by the sweep (`via reconcile`) without paging. A failed sweep run neither counts nor breaks the streak.
  - Replayed events are left out of the delay, because they're late by design.
- **11.4 Number 3, Salesforce API failure rate:** a table of what counts.
  - **R3:** timeouts, `5xx`, and `4xx` other than `412` and `429` all count, and retries are included in the total. Above 5% pages. There's a separate 1% threshold for validation or permission rejections. `412` and `429` are tracked separately.
  - It isn't evaluated while the breaker is open, and outage probes are left out after it closes.
- **11.5:** the other pages already decided elsewhere (missing watermark, conflicting `sf_id`, unrecoverable replay window), tied back to the three numbers.
- **11.6:** what the three numbers don't catch, and where each of those shows up instead.

**One detail I added to R2:** a change only counts as missed if it was made **more than 60 s before** the sweep read it. # Tequity Round 1 - Salesforce <-> portal sync

Design docs live in `docs/`: decisions in `decisions.tmp.md`, assumptions in `assumptions.md`,
build order in `subproblems.md`. Decision labels (`Dn`, `Sn`) point into `decisions.tmp.md`.

## Shared database and `saveEdit()` module (decision S4) - keep these rules when changing code

The portal backend, the webhook receiver and the sync worker share one Postgres database. A portal
edit writes the record, its history and the outbox row in **one transaction** through a shared
`saveEdit()` module. That transaction is what stops a crash from losing an edit or sending an
unsaved one (D23). The costs we accepted, and the rules that contain them:

1. **Every portal write goes through `saveEdit()`.** A direct `UPDATE` on a records table skips the
   outbox, and that edit silently never reaches Salesforce. A test must fail if a record row changes
   without a matching outbox row. Never bypass it, even for scripts or admin fixes.
2. **The webhook path never writes to the outbox** (loop rule, D17). Do not add a database trigger
   that writes the outbox on every update: it would also fire on webhook writes.
3. **Sync tables live in their own `sync` schema** (`inbox`, `outbox`, `jobs`). The sync code owns
   their migrations; the portal only calls the module.
4. **Same language:** the module is TypeScript on Node (20+), the portal backend's language.
5. **Each service has its own capped connection pool** (e.g. receiver 10, worker 5), so a webhook
   burst or an outage drain cannot starve portal users.
6. **A failed outbox insert fails the user's save.** This is deliberate: a save that cannot be
   synced must not look saved.
7. **One Postgres role per service, least privilege.** For example, the receiver cannot touch
   `outbox`; the worker never receives HTTP; the receiver never calls Salesforce (D22).

## Locking and the Salesforce precondition (decisions G1, G2, G2b) - keep these rules

1. **Every write to per-field state goes through `withRecordLock(recordId, fn)`**: lock the record row
   (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), read, run the pure apply function, write, commit. No other way to open a
   transaction on records.
2. **Never call Salesforce inside a transaction.** The Salesforce client throws when called inside
   `withRecordLock`; keep that check and its test. The worker sends in three steps: claim (tx) -> HTTP
   call (no tx) -> store result (tx).
3. **Lock order:** customer before contact, then by ID. Deadlock victims retry.
4. **One record per transaction** for replay, drain and sweep. Bulk work (e.g. linking contacts to a
   newly arrived customer) runs in batches of 500, each its own transaction.
5. **Keep transactions to database writes only.** Emails, HTTP calls and other side effects happen
   after the commit.
6. **Postgres timeouts per role:** `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 5s`, `lock_timeout = 2s`,
   `statement_timeout = 5s`. Migrations use their own role with a `lock_timeout`.
7. **Every update to Salesforce is conditional on `sf_seq_contiguous`** (the highest sequence with no
   gap below it), never on `sf_seq_max`: a missing webhook below our version must cause a `412`, not a
   stale write. On `412`: no GET. Wait 5 s for in-flight webhooks; if `sf_seq_contiguous` has not
   passed `base_version`, run a `replay_record` job; then re-run the guard on exact per-field times and
   resend only the winners. Our own landed write is recognised by an event carrying its key `ob_<id>.<content_gen>`. Never retry a
   lost field automatically; the user overrides with "Use my value again".
8. **Replay restarts from the oldest completed sweep watermark minus 10 minutes**, never from "the last
   `eventId` we applied" (webhooks arrive out of order) and never from the heartbeat (it keeps beating
   during a Salesforce outage). A sweep watermark advances only after a run's last page is applied, or
   when a replay completes; a missing watermark means "replay from the retention limit" and pages (Q10a).
9. **A contact is never sent before its customer has an `sf_id`**; the claim parks it, and
   `link_contacts` (queued by whatever sets the customer's `sf_id`) wakes it.
10. **At most one `sending` outbox row per record** (unique partial index). A `sending` row's content
    and key are frozen; after a timeout, `5xx` or `412` it stays `sending` and never returns to
    `pending`. Only evidence (an event with its key, or a full replay without it) decides whether an
    uncertain attempt landed (`docs/outbound.md` 6.6).
11. **Revert and guard by `editId`, never by value.** A field is reverted or sent only if
    `field_meta.editId` still equals the outbox field's `editId`. One resend after a rejection, never a
    third attempt; never revert a rejected create.

## Other fixed rules

- Only one sync worker is active at a time (Postgres advisory lock, standby takes over). The rate
  limiter is in memory; do not scale the worker horizontally without a shared limiter.
- Contact full name is stored as `first_name` / `last_name` (Salesforce `Contact.Name` is read-only).
- **`history` is append-only:** insert, never update or delete (old partitions are archived, not
  deleted). `superseded` is set at insert time by the apply rule.
- **`field_meta` (JSONB) has no database-enforced shape:** only the apply function writes it, and it
  validates `{updatedAt, source, actor, sfSeq, sfValue}` for every field. Table layouts are in
  `docs/data.md`.
- **`sfSeq` and `sfValue` only move forward:** webhooks, echoes, replies, fetches and sweeps update them
  only when their sequence is newer. An echo kept as sent never changes the field's `actor` or
  `updatedAt` and writes no history row (I1, `docs/inbound.md` 5.2).
- **Inbound record lookup order is `sf_id` -> `id = Portal_Id__c` (adopt if `sf_id` NULL) -> create**
  (I2, `docs/inbound.md` 5.3). Never insert a record for a webhook before trying `Portal_Id__c`, or a
  portal create whose reply was lost becomes two rows.
- **At most one pending outbox row per record**, enforced by a unique partial index; merge with
  `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`, never a second pending row.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types. This does not cover the `web-fetch` agent type where it is listed and you have no WebFetch tool of your own: it stands in for that tool, so calling it to read a page is ordinary tool use.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
